Democrats win control of the House of Representatives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
03:36:23 UTC
12:36:23 KST

Democrats won control of the House of Representatives with what could be their largest majority in nearly two decades, NBC News projects, as voters delivered a stunning rebuke to President Donald Trump and Republicans.
The House projection is based on an analysis that Democrats will win approximately 248 House seats — an estimate that could still tick up or down by a few seats but will be well beyond the 218 needed to secure a majority.
NBC News has not yet projected who will win the Senate.
Democrats needed to win a net of just three seats to take back the majority. They flipped many more GOP-held seats, most in districts that Trump carried in the 2024 election.
A trio of GOP incumbents in Pennsylvania were defeated. Democrat Bob Brooks knocked off GOP Rep. Ryan Mackenzie in the 7th Congressional District; Paige Cognetti beat GOP Rep. Rob Bresnahan in the 8th District; and Democrat Janelle Stelson ousted GOP Rep. Scott Perry in the 10th District.
In Virginia, Democratic former Rep. Elaine Luria won back her old seat, defeating Republican Rep. Jen Kiggans in the Virginia Beach area.
In Colorado, Democratic state Rep. Manny Rutinel defeated GOP Rep. Gabe Evans.
And in North Carolina, farmer Jamie Ager defeated GOP state Rep. Jennifer Balkcom in a district Trump won two years ago by more than 9 percentage points.
Balkcom took over as the GOP nominee after Republican Rep. Chuck Edwards dropped his bid for re-election following harassment allegations.
The Democrats’ victory was widely seen as a referendum on Trump’s unpopular policies, including his tough immigration crackdown, the eight-month Iran war and tariffs on U.S. allies that drove up the price of gas, groceries and other goods.
When the party takes control of the chamber on Jan. 3, it will mark the first time in Trump’s second term that he won’t have full control of Congress. Since he returned to the White House, Trump has tested the limits of his executive powers, dismantling federal agencies cuts through the Department of Government Efficiency, unilaterally imposing sweeping tariffs and rescinding congressionally approved funding — all while the GOP-controlled House and Senate mostly looked the other way.
Follow live updates on the midterm elections
The House Democratic leader, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who barnstormed across the country in the final weeks of the campaign, is expected to make history on Jan. 3 when he is sworn in as the first Black speaker of the House.
With their new majority, Democrats will take control of House committees, gaining subpoena power and the ability to conduct oversight investigations into Trump’s administration, family and business ventures. That could take up considerable time and resources for Trump and his allies, forcing uncomfortable public hearings or prompting legal showdowns over subpoenas.
And in a callback to Trump’s first term, some Democrats have vowed to impeach him for a third time, though there is an internal debate about whether that’s the right political path.
Jeffries told NBC News’ “Meet the Press” that Democrats “haven’t ruled anything in and we haven’t ruled anything out” on impeachment.
Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., now poised to become chairman of the powerful Oversight Committee in January, said his panel plans to focus on “Trump family corruption,” including Trump’s cryptocurrency ventures, which have earned him more than $1 billion. The panel will also scrutinize “abuses” by ICE and the Department of Homeland Security, corporate corruption and the Jeffrey Epstein files.
Aside from investigative power, House Democrats will also command the ability to pass legislation with a simple majority. Jeffries has said Democrats would focus on four areas: reversing Trump’s cuts to Medicaid, extending the Affordable Care Act credits, restoring congressional authority related to tariffs and stopping Trump’s war with Iran.
“I wouldn’t characterize it as investigating them like crazy. We’re going to follow the facts, apply the law, be guided by the Constitution and let the chips fall where they may,” Jeffries told reporters at Democrats’ campaign headquarters before the election.
The results are a blow to Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., who was launched from obscurity into the top job and has led House Republicans for the past three years. It’s unclear whether Johnson, a close Trump ally, will fight to remain as minority leader or step aside; the latter would trigger a fiercely competitive GOP race to replace him.
House Democrats had the political wind at their backs; they needed to flip a net of just three seats to win back the majority they lost in 2022. And Trump’s dismal approval rating was a major factor in the GOP’s loss.
Historically, the president’s party tends to lose seats in midterm elections. Only in two midterms in the modern era did a party buck that trend — in 1998, when voters punished Republicans for impeaching President Bill Clinton, and in 2002, as President George W. Bush rallied support in the wake of the 9/11 terrorist attacks.
Still, the battle for House control played out primarily on GOP turf this cycle, with Democrats already holding 215 seats, including a dozen in battleground districts. On top of that, results of this cycle’s mid-decade redistricting wars ended up favoring Republicans slightly, though Democrats quickly moved to neutralize what could have been a large GOP advantage.
Trump fired the first shot in the summer of 2025, when he urged GOP allies in Texas to redraw their congressional lines to help the party pick up as many as five seats. Republicans also redrew maps in places like Florida, North Carolina, Tennessee, Alabama, Louisiana and Missouri in a bid to win more seats.
But Democrats countered in California, with Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Speaker Nancy Pelosi and their allies successfully rallying support for Proposition 50, which approved a new congressional map drawn by state Democrats. That map helped Democrats pick up GOP-held seats.
While the GOP successfully picked up a handful of majority-Black, Democratic-held seats in the South, the Supreme Court blocked Missouri Republicans’ new congressional map, essentially preserving the Kansas City seat of longtime Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.
“We made a promise to aggressively push back against the MAGA extremist effort to rip the election away from the American people by gerrymandering the possibility of Democrats winning the majority out of existence,” Jeffries said before the election, adding that the redistricting wars will continue in the 120th Congress.
“This fight is not over; we’ve just gotten started,” he added. “It will continue into the next Congress until we pass legislation signed into law by a future president that will prohibit mid-decade gerrymandering from ever happening again.”

Ukraine's Drone Strikes Spur Hasty Russian Plans For Underground Data Centers

Ukraine's Drone Strikes Spur Hasty Russian Plans For Underground Data Centers (arstechnica.com) 3
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: [S]tate-owned telecommunications company Rostelcom has raised the possibility of moving some Russian data centers underground in talks with the nickel and palladium mining company Norilsk, according to Russian newspaper Vedomosti. The industry publication Data Center Dynamics also pointed to a recent proposal by a Russian regional governor to build data centers within open-pit coal mines while planting green public parks above as camouflage.
On November 2, Putin also signed a decree ordering Russian data center operators to set aside 10 percent of available space and capacity in case the Russian government requires it, according to independent Russian news publication Meduza. That may indicate growing Kremlin concerns about the vulnerability of Russian cloud computing infrastructure during its war with Ukraine. Putin's decree also allows a special Russian government commission to authorize use of foreign data centers in consultation with Russia's Federal Security Service. That marks a notable policy change because Putin and the Russian parliament previously enacted Russia's "Sovereign Internet Law," which has blocked Russian companies from using cloud computing infrastructure outside Russia's borders.
Russia's push for a sovereign and increasingly closed Internet has resulted in a highly centralized system under a few Russian tech companies like Yandex. That hyper-centralized system has now proven vulnerable during wartime, as Ukrainian drone strikes on key Russian data centers created widespread disruptions for popular payment and digital banking apps, e-commerce platforms, video streaming services, and ride-hailing and food delivery apps, among others. Yandex has also been forced to relocate all three of its main supercomputers after Ukrainian drone strikes targeted the AI data centers where they were originally housed, Meduza reported.

Arrows to arrows, categories to queries (2025)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
03:11:27 UTC
12:11:27 KST

Arrows to Arrows, Categories to Queries
I’ve had a little time off of work as of late, and been spending it in characteristically unwise ways. In particular, I’ve written a little programming language that compiles to SQL. I call it catlang. That’s not to say that I’ve written a new query language. It’s a programming language, whose compiler spits out one giant SELECT statement. When you run that query in postgres, you get the output of your program.
Why have I done this? Because I needed a funny compilation target to test out the actual features of the language, which is that its intermediary language is a bunch of abstract category theory nonsense. Which I’ll get to. But I’m sure you first want to see this bad boy in action.
Behold, the function that returns 100 regardless of what input you give it. But it does it with the equivalent of a while loop:
count : Int -> Int
count =
  x ->
    loop x
      i ->
        n <- join id id -< i
        z <- abs . (-) -< (n, 100)
        case z of
          inl _ -> inr . (+) -< (n, 1)
          inr _ -> inl -< n
If you’re familiar with arrow notation, you’ll notice the above looks kinda like one big proc block. This is not a coincidence (because nothing is a coincidence). I figured if I were to go through all of this work, we might as well get a working arrow desugarer out of the mix. But I digress; that’s a story for another time.
Anyway, what’s going on here is we have an arrow count, which takes a single argument x. We then loop, starting from the value of x. Inside the loop, we now have a new variable i, which we do some voodoo on to compute n—the current value of the loop variable. Then we subtract 100 from n, and take the absolute value. The abs function here is a bit odd; it returns Left (abs x) if the input was negative, and Right x otherwise. Then we branch on the output of abs, where Left and Right have been renamed inl and inr respectively. If n - 100 was less than zero, we find ourselves in the inl case, where we add 1 to n and wrap the whole thing in inr—which the loop interprets as “loop again with this new value.” Otherwise, n - 100 was non-negative, and so we can return n directly.
Is it roundabout? You bet! The obtuseness here is not directly a feature, I was just looking for conceptually simple things I could do which would be easy to desugar into category-theoretical stuff. Which brings us to the intermediary language. After desugaring the source syntax for count above, we’re left with this IL representation:
  id △ id
⨟ cochoice
    ( undist
    ⨟   ( (prj₁ ⨟ id ▽ id) △ id
          ⨟   ( prj₁ △ 100
              ⨟ (-)
              ⨟ abs
              )
            △ id
          ⨟ prj₁ △ id
          ⨟ dist
          ⨟   ( (prj₂ ⨟ prj₂ ⨟ prj₁) △ 1
              ⨟ (+)
              ⨟ inr
              )
            ▽ ( prj₂
              ⨟ prj₂
              ⨟ prj₁
              ⨟ inl
              )
        )
      △ prj₂
    ⨟ dist
    )
⨟ prj₁
We’ll discuss all of this momentarily, but for now, just let your eyes glaze over the pretty unicode.
The underlying idea here is that each of these remaining symbols has very simple and specific algebraic semantics. For example, A ⨟ B means “do A and pipe the result into B.” By giving a transformation from this categorical IL into other domains, it becomes trivial to compile catlang to all sorts of weird compilation targets. Like SQL.
You’re probably wondering what the generated SQL looks like. Take a peek if you dare.

It’s not pretty, rather amazingly, running the above query in postgres 17 will in fact return a single row with a single column whose value is 100. And you’d better believe it does it by actually looping its way up to 100. If you don’t believe me, make the following change:
-     SELECT * FROM recursion ORDER BY step DESC LIMIT 1)
+     SELECT * FROM recursion ORDER BY step DESC)
which will instead return a row for each step of the iteration.
There are some obvious optimizations I could make to the generated SQL, but it didn’t seem worth my time, since that’s not the interesting part of the project.
What the Hell Is Going On?
Let’s take some time to discuss the underlying category theory here. I am by no means an expert, but what I have learned after a decade of bashing my head against this stuff is that a little goes a long way.
For our intents and purposes, we have types, and arrows (functions) between types. We always have the identity “do nothing arrow” id:
id  :: a ~> a
and we can compose arrows by lining up one end to another:1
(⨟) :: (a ~> b) -> (b ~> c) -> (a ~> c)
Unlike Haskell (or really any programming language, for that matter), we DO NOT have the notion of function application. That is, there is no arrow:
-- doesn't exist!
($) :: (a ~> b) -> a -> b
You can only compose arrows, you can’t apply them. That’s why we call these things “arrows” rather than “functions.”
There are a bundle of arrows for working with product types. The two projection functions correspond to fst and snd, taking individual components out of pairs:
prj₁ :: (a, b) ~> a
prj₂ :: (a, b) ~> b
How do we get things into pairs in the first place? We can use the “fork” operation, which takes two arrows computing b and c, and generates a new arrow which generates a pair of (b, c):
(△)  :: (a ~> b) -> (a ~> c) -> (a ~> (b, c))
If you’re coming from a Haskell background, it’s tempting to think of this operation merely as the (,) pair constructor. But you’ll notice from the type of the computation that there can be no data dependency between b and c, thus we are free to parallelize each side of the pair.
In category theory, the distinction between left and right sides of an arrow is rather arbitrary. This gives rise to a notion called duality where we can flip the arrows around, and get cool new behavior. If we dualize all of our product machinery, we get the coproduct machinery, where a coproduct of a and b is “either a or b, but definitely not both nor neither.”
Swapping the arrow direction of prj₁ and prj₂, and replacing (,) with Either gives us the following injections:
inl :: a ~> Either a b
inr :: b ~> Either a b
and the following “join” operation for eliminating coproducts:
(▽) :: (a ~> c) -> (b ~> c) -> (Either a b ~> c)
Again, coming from Haskell this is just the standard either function. It corresponds to a branch between one of two cases.
As you can see, with just these eight operations, we already have a tremendous amount of expressivity. We can express data dependencies via ⨟ and branching via ▽. With △ we automatically encode opportunities for parallelism, and gain the ability to build complicated data structures, with prj₁ and prj₂ allowing us to get the information back out of the data structures.
You’ll notice in the IL that there are no variable names anywhere to be found. The desugaring of the source language builds a stack (via the something to allocate △ id pattern), and replaces subsequent variable lookups with a series of projections on the stack to find the value again. On one hand, this makes the categorical IL rather hard to read, but it makes it very easy to re-target! Many domains do have a notion of grouping, but don’t have a native notion of naming.
For example, in an electronic circuit, I can have a ribbon of 32 wires which represents an Int32. If I have another ribbon of 32 wires, I can trivially route both wires into a 64-wire ribbon corresponding to a pair of (Int32, Int32).
By eliminating names before we get to the IL, it means no compiler backend ever needs to deal with names. They can just work on a stack representation, and are free to special-case optimize series of projections if they are able to.
Of particular interest to this discussion is how we desugar loops in catlang. The underlying primitive is cochoice:
cochoice :: (Either a c ~> Either b c) -> (a ~> b)
which magically turns an arrow on Eithers into an arrow without the eithers. We obviously must run that arrow on eithers. If that function returns inl, then we’re happy and we can just output that. But if the function returns inr, we have no choice but to pass it back in to the eithered arrow. In Haskell, cochoice is implemented as:
cochoiceHask :: (Either a c -> Either b c) -> a -> c
cochoiceHask f = go . Left
  where
    go :: Either a c -> b
    go eac =
      case f eac of
        Left b -> b
        Right c -> go (Right c)
which as you can see, will loop until f finally returns a Left. What’s neat about this formulation of a loop is that we can statically differentiate between our first and subsequent passes through the loop body. The first time through eac is Left, while for all other times it is Right. We don’t take advantage of it in the original count program, but how many times have you written loop code that needs to initialize something its first time through?
Compiling to SQL
So that’s the underlying theory behind the IL. How can we compile this to SQL now?
As alluded to before, we simply need to give SQL implementations for each of the operations in the intermediary language. As a simple example, id compiles to SELECT * FROM {}, where {} is the input of the arrow.
The hardest part here was working out a data representation. It seems obvious to encode each element of a product as a new column, but what do we do about coproducts? After much work thought, I decided to flatten out the coproducts. So, for example, the type:
(Int, Either Int Int)
would be represented as three columns:
( f1 INT NOT NULL
, f2 INT
, f3 INT
)
with the constraint that exactly one of f2 or f3 would be IS NOT NULL at any given point in time.
With this hammered out, almost everything else is pretty trivial. Composition corresponds to a nested query. Forks are CROSS JOINs which concatenate the columns of each sub-query. Joins are UNIONs, where we add a WHERE field IS NOT NULL clause to enforce we’re looking at the correct coproduct constructor.
Cochoice is the only really tricky thing, but it corresponds to a recursive CTE. Generating a recursive CTE table for the computation isn’t too hard, but getting the final value out of it was surprisingly tricky. The semantics of SQL tables is that they are multisets and come with an arbitrary greatest element. Which is to say, you need an column structured in a relevant way in order to query the final result. Due to some quirks in what postgres accepts, and in how I structured my queries, it was prohibitively hard to insert a “how many times have I looped” column and order by that. So instead I cheated and added a clock_timestamp() as step column which looks at the processor clock and ordered by that.
This is clearly a hack, and presumably will cause problems if I ever add some primitives which generate more than one row, but again, this is just for fun and who cares. Send me a pull request if you’re offended by my chicanery!
Stupid Directions To Go In the Future
I’ve run out of vacation time to work on this project, so I’m probably not going to get around to the meta-circular stupidity I was planning.
The compiler still needs a few string-crunching primitives (which are easy to add), but then it would be simple to write a little brainfuck interpreter in catlang. Which I could then compile to SQL. Now we’ve got a brainfuck interpreter running in postgres. Of course, this has been done by hand before, but to my knowledge, never via compilation.
There exist C to brainfuck compilers. And postgres is written in C. So in a move that would make Xzibit proud, we could run postgres in postgres. And of course, it would be fun to run brainfuck in brainfuck. That’d be a cool catlang backend if someone wanted to contribute such a thing.
Notes and Due Diligence and What Have You
I am not the first person to do anything like this. The source language of catlang is heavily inspired by Haskell’s arrow syntax, which in turn is essentially a desugaring algorithm for Arrows. Arrows are slightly the wrong abstraction because they require an operation arr :: (a -> b) -> (a ~> b)—which requires you to be able to embed Haskell functions in your category, something which is almost never possible.
Unfortunately, arrow syntax in Haskell desugars down to arr for almost everything it does, which in turn makes arrow notation effectively useless. In an ideal world, everything I described in this blog post would be a tiny little Haskell library, with arrow notation doing the heavy lifting. But that is just not the world we live in.
Nor am I the first person to notice that there are categorical semantics behind programming languages. I don’t actually know whom to cite on this one, but it is well-established folklore that the lambda calculus corresponds to cartesian-closed categories. The “closed” part of “cartesian-closed” means we have an operation eval :: (a ~> b, a) ~> b, but everyone and their dog has implemented the lambda calculus, so I thought it would be fun to see how far we can get without it. This is not a limitation on catlang’s turing completeness (since cochoice gives us everything we need.)
I’ve been thinking about writing a category-first programming language for the better part of a decade, ever since I read Compiling to Categories. That paper takes Haskell and desugars it back down to categories. I stole many of the tricks here from that paper.
Anyway. All of the code is available on github if you’re interested in taking a look. The repo isn’t up to my usual coding standards, for which you have my apologies. Of note is the template-haskell backend which can spit out Haskell code; meaning it wouldn’t be very hard to make a quasiquoter to compile catlang into what Haskell’s arrow desugaring ought to be. If there’s enough clamor for such a thing, I’ll see about turning this part into a library.
- When looking at the types of arrows in this essay, we make the distinction that ~> are arrows that we can write in catlang, while -> exist in the metatheory.↩︎

AMD CEO Lisa Su said in the company’s quarterly earnings call on Tuesday that Q3 2026 was “was the largest and most profitable in our history.” AMD reported a record $13.4 billion in quarterly revenue, and it’s predicting it will hit another record high next quarter of $17 billion. The company’s data center business is driving that growth, with $8.5 billion in data center quarterly revenue for Q3 2026. Su said AMD’s expecting its revenue to “grow more than 80 percent in 2027,” adding that “data center will be the largest contributor.”
AMD rides data center riches to ‘largest and most profitable’ quarter in history
AMD thinks over 80 percent of its revenue will eventually come from its data center business alone.
Eventually, most of AMD’s revenue might come from its data center business. In response to a question during Tuesday’s earnings call, CFO Jean Hu said, “Looking ahead of 2027, we actually think our data center business will be more than 80 percent of total company revenue.”
As of Q3 2026, roughly 63 percent of AMD’s net quarterly revenue was from its data center business. Over the last couple years, jumps in the company’s revenue have been closely mirroring its data center business — in Q3 2026 its overall revenue went up $1.9 billion, while its data center revenue went up $1.8 billion.
As AMD keeps smashing its data center revenue records, its gaming business dropped 40 percent compared to last year, dipping to $773 million. PCs, game consoles, and other tech have been hit with price hikes over recent months due to shortages of RAM and other components, driven by demand from AI data centers. The shortage might not end anytime soon — Intel said it’s not expecting the shortage to improve next year, and SK Hynix predicted it’ll last until 2030.
Su acknowledged the price hikes, saying, “Our view is, this is one of those times — when, you know, component prices go up, it affects overall system pricing. One would expect the consumer markets to be more sensitive to that, and so we have seen a bit of a slowdown in the sell-through.” Su added, “We are planning with the current environment for a down year for 2027.”

The biggest modding site in PC gaming is taking a stance on AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04

The PC gaming mods repository Nexus Mods is making disclosures about AI mandatory for uploads of new mods, meaning that mod authors will have to declare “whether AI has been used in their work,” the site announced today as part of a big post about AI-generated content on the platform.
The biggest modding site in PC gaming is taking a stance on AI
Nexus Mods says that authors of newly uploaded mods will have to declare whether AI was ‘used in their work.’
“One of the most consistent concerns we’ve heard is that it’s not clearly disclosed when AI has been used to create a mod,” according to the post from site owner Victor “Foledinho” Folmann. “We already have tags for AI-generated and AI-assisted mods, but we recognise that there’s a lot more we can do to make that information more accessible and clear for you all.” Any mods tagged as “AI-assisted” will also be required to include “a public explanation of how and where AI was used.” AI tags will also be “more prominent” on mod pages.
Folmann says Nexus Mods is “pro-human creativity” but “won’t introduce an outright ban on AI-generated mods.” As for why that is:
The answer is simple: AI is currently used throughout the whole process of creation, from script autocompletion to generation of textures, voices, and full assets, and it is difficult to draw a clear boundary between what is acceptable and unacceptable. An outright ban will not eliminate AI from the modding process but will prevent people from mentioning its use. We’d prefer the opposite; it should be out in the open, clearly labelled, and regulated according to the rules that we can implement on our platform.
Folmann notes that Nexus Mods won’t use mods to train AI and “will not sell or license them to anyone doing so.” However, the site is working on “clearer control” over how mods can be reused on others and strengthening attribution for when “a mod uses another Mod Author’s mod with the appropriate permissions.”
Nexus Mods is also making changes to the Recently Added section of the site to address a problem of mod authors uploading many mods at once, which makes other mods fall down down the page. “This is less of an issue related to AI, but it’s becoming much more prevalent as mod production is speeding up,” Folmann says. The changes include trying limits on how many mods from one author are shown at a time and “tighter restrictions” on uploads from new accounts. The platform is also launching controls to hide AI-generated content in game pages and on the homepage, and “next up,” in search.
Nexus Mods’ full AI policy is here, and mod authors have 60 days to update their existing mods to meet the requirements. The 60-day grace period ends on January 2nd, and after that time, the site will begin enforcing the rules.

C++26 Disapproved
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-04
00:33:22 UTC
09:33:22 KST

C++26 DIS failed, how does C++ survive?
On October 23, 2026, the unthinkable happened. It was supposed to be a mere formality: C++26 was up for a vote by the ISO National Bodies (NBs). The options are always approval, rejection, or abstention. Comments are also allowed. Since 1998, this process had run quietly and smoothly. Not so on October 23, 2026. After a twelve-week voting period, the result is in: Disapproved!
I would like to mention here that I am a member of the C++ Standardization Committee and, together with my colleagues, represent Germany’s vote. ISO rules also stipulate that certain votes are internal to ISO, and the results—or the breakdown of the results—may not be published. This article contains my own personal views.
The Current Status
As far as I know, this is the first time in the history of C++ that DIS ballot failed. When I searched the ISO system, I could only find one other DIS that was not approved: ISO/IEC DIS 26926 C++/CLI Language Specification dated August 11, 2006. It’s possible that my search privileges aren’t sufficient to view everything, but all ISO programming languages should be visible to me. The sad end of ISO/IEC DIS 26926: the project was halted. I mention this upfront to clarify the significance of this vote.
In the following, I will use various terms from everyday ISO terminology. At https://isocpp.org/std/iso-iec-jtc1-procedures, there is an overview of the various stages of an ISO standard. DIS is the penultimate stage. As the overview also shows, a two-thirds majority is required. This majority was not achieved.
The reason for the rejection is quite clear from the comments submitted by the National Bodies (NBs): contracts. Put simply, a number of NBs believe that this feature is not yet ready for release.
The Process
Now it gets complicated. The C++ Standardization Committee, also known as WG21, follows ISO rules but also has some additional rules. One of these is (or was) that opinions are always heard whenever new information becomes available. If an opinion was heard and a feature was nevertheless not changed as desired, the person respects the outcome and accepts that many others disagree.
However, the voting body at the NB level may also consist of other individuals, or the NBs are, of course, free to vote differently.
The previous practice was that NBs would only vote against a standard if new information became available or if errors in the process or similar issues were identified. This changed on October 23, 2026.
It’s difficult to judge in this complex situation; the NBs who want C++26 without Contracts argue that there is new information. I myself find it hard to share this view. A new paper with old arguments is not new information to me.
The History of Contracts in C++
The feature has been on the wish list for a long time. I was already in the room in Cologne back in 2019, at the time for C++20, when Contracts, in a different form back then, were being included in the standard. I was also in the room when the feature was removed from C++20 again during the same meeting. As a result, a study group was formed to address the topic of Contracts and its various aspects from 2020 to approximately 2024. Afterward, the study group submitted its work and proposals to the Evolution Working Group (EWG), the central body for language extensions. There, the topic was discussed further over several meetings before being included in C++26 by a majority vote.
In the next step, WG21 voted on the C++26 draft in March 2026, which included Contracts. Here, too, a large majority was achieved, though not without dissenting votes.
And that brings us to the next phase: DIS. At this stage, there were enough “no” votes that a two-thirds majority was not reached.
What happens next?
The big problem: what happens next? ISO, of course, has a process for this. It offers various options:
- Submit a revised draft for a new DIS vote.
- Submit a revised draft to the committee (that would be the CD phase).
- Publish a revised draft as a Technical Specification.
- Cancel the project.
All of these possibilities mean a delay in the next C++ standard. Whether it will still be called C++26 is also up in the air, but that’s a much smaller issue.
The difficulty with all four options is that they require a majority within WG21. However, this working group voted to move C++26 with Contracts into the next voting phase leading to its release. And it did so with more than just the required two-thirds majority. The feature didn’t come out of nowhere, either; it was developed over the course of years through the work and possibly personal commitment of many people. It’s hard to imagine that this group would simply want to abandon its work, which has received approval on multiple occasions so far. The same applies to the group that is dissatisfied with Contracts. This group, too, has invested effort, in some cases even in alternative implementations. It’s hard to imagine that, after these groups voted “no” in the DIS vote, the result would change without Contracts being removed.
Even the last option removing C++26 requires a majority in WG21. As I understand it, this step would mean reverting to C++23 and proceeding to C++29 without a single change. This would affect the work of even more people. WG21 would then be tasked with incorporating features that have already been successfully included in C++26 into C++29. Since this can only be done through a paper backed by at least one person advocating for it, features could be omitted if that person lacks the motivation or time.
Of course, certainty about the voting outcome can only be achieved if the respective path is actually taken.
Unfortunately, the way forward is currently more than uncertain. Perhaps this also explains why ISO/IEC DIS 26926 marked the end of this activity. Consensus is needed to move forward. Trust is always required for consensus. Unfortunately, that trust has just been shaken.
The next C++ standard, and thus the future of C++, is currently at an impasse.
The good news is that the next meeting will take place on November 16, which is just a few days away. The top priority will be to break the deadlock. This will very likely have implications for C++29 as well; in fact, there is currently no reason to continue working on this project.
My Personal Opinion
Normally, my articles are technically focused and free of personal opinion. Regarding the rejected DIS, I can only say that I consider it a massive disaster and feel sorry for the entire C++ community. Regardless of whether someone likes Contracts, considers them important, or sees major weaknesses in them, the topic has been worked on for years and has received a majority vote multiple times in its current form. By voting “no,” an established system, one based primarily on trust and respectful collaboration, has been shaken. Every ISO standard is simply a set of compromises. Everyone loses sometimes, and everyone wins sometimes. Overall, the result is one in which all participants have given their best. During the DIS vote, the losing parties refused to accept their loss. The question that primarily determines how to move forward is whether the group can rebuild trust.
Andreas

[...] Apple is adding Adaptive Dark Mode for websites that don't have a dark mode design option by default. If you use Dark Mode and then browse to a website with a bright background color, Safari will offer an option to "Try" Adaptive Dark Mode. After tapping Try, Safari renders a Dark Mode version of the page that makes the background darker, changes text contrast, inverts logos and graphics, recolors vector artwork, lifts raised surfaces, and rebalances layered shadows.
Each website will be adapted based on what's needed to make it readable, so not every tweak is applied to every site. You can opt to turn Adaptive Dark Mode on for all sites or on a site-by-site basis after using it. If a site has a native dark mode or has a dark design already, Adaptive Dark Mode won't activate. Developers can also add a tag that causes Safari to ignore Adaptive Dark Mode and show the website as the developer intended.

Prompting Is Programming
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
23:49:06 UTC
08:49:06 KST

Prompting Is Programming
The other day I watched a friend of mine, an Ivy League-educated professor in the liberal arts, work with Claude. The conversation went in circles, and they never articulated what their goal was. Each reply from Claude was reasonable given what it had been told, and each one was a little off from what my friend actually wanted, so they’d nudge it, and it would drift somewhere else. This is one of the smartest people I know, and I was watching them struggle with a tool that has completely reshaped the way I build software.
That interaction came to mind when I was reading about how industries outside of software aren’t seeing productivity gains from AI. Marketers, analysts, managers, and operations folks get some help drafting emails and summarizing meetings, then spend the time they saved cleaning up plausible-looking output that doesn’t quite do what they needed. The org-wide productivity gains that were promised mostly haven’t materialized. For software engineers, the change is night and day. I basically stopped writing code within a few weeks of Opus 4.5 shipping, and nearly every engineer I know has a version of that story.
The usual explanations are that the models were trained on mountains of code, that code is verifiable because it either compiles and passes the tests or it doesn’t, and that the AI labs poured their best tooling effort into coding agents because their own employees are engineers. All of that is true. None of it fully explains the gap, because I’ve watched other engineers, and experienced it myself, get great results out of these tools on tasks that have nothing to do with code, like planning a trip, restructuring a budget, or drafting a grant proposal.
My theory is simpler. Prompting an AI well is programming. The mental work is the same; only the syntax changed. Engineers are good at it because they’ve spent years doing it, and most other people haven’t done it at all.
Consider what goes through your mind when you write a function or class. You decide what the inputs are and where they come from. You decide exactly what the output should look like. You break the problem into steps small enough that each one is obviously right. You think about the edge cases: the empty list, the missing field, the user who does something you didn’t expect. You decide how you’ll know it works. None of that is about typing semicolons, and all of it is what separates a good prompt from a bad one. A starting state and a goal state are the first things a programmer writes down, even if only in their head. They were exactly what was missing from my friend’s session.
A non-programmer asks the agent to “put together a report on Q3 sales.” An engineer, without really thinking about it, asks a different question: which data, in which file, broken down by what, compared against what baseline, in what format, and what should happen with the two regions that reorganized mid-quarter? The engineer isn’t smarter. My friend could run circles around most engineers I know intellectually. The engineer has just had the precision beaten into them by a compiler.
Every programmer spent years being told, instantly and without mercy, that the computer does what you said rather than what you meant. Non-programmers have spent their careers communicating with humans, who fill in the gaps with shared context and common sense, and who come back with a clarifying question when they’re confused. An LLM also fills in the gaps, but it fills them with the most plausible guess and rarely asks. A vague prompt doesn’t throw an error. The model hallucinates what you meant, hands back something that looks about right, and leaves you to discover where it isn’t. An engineer’s instinct is to distrust output that looks about right. Most people’s instinct is to accept it.
The gap gets wider when the output is wrong. An engineer debugs. They form a hypothesis about which part of their instructions led the model astray, change that one thing, and run it again. A non-programmer tends to reroll the same prompt, append “please be accurate,” or conclude that the tool doesn’t work. They’ve never had to build the habit of treating a bad result as information about their own input.
This complicates something I wrote in May. I argued that domain expertise is the real moat, and that a domain expert with an agent can be startlingly effective because they know what right looks like. I still believe the oracle matters. But knowing what right looks like is a judging skill, and it only kicks in once the agent has produced something worth judging. Getting it there is a specifying skill, and that one is computational. When I look at the non-engineers who really are getting enormous value from these tools, they almost always have a programmer’s brain hiding under a different job title: the finance person who builds elaborate spreadsheets with lookup tables, the ops manager who writes their own Zapier flows, the researcher who wrangles data in R because nobody else would. They were programming all along. They just didn’t call it that.
Which brings me back to my friend. They didn’t need a better prompt template or a list of magic phrases. They needed the habits any second-year computer science student has without thinking about them: say what done looks like before you start, break the work into pieces small enough to check, and when the answer comes back wrong, ask what in your own instructions sent it there. None of that requires knowing a programming language. It does require years of being corrected by a compiler, and most brilliant people have never spent a single afternoon on the receiving end of one.
Natural language programming was sold as a way to let everyone program. So far it mostly lets people who already think like programmers do it faster, in English.

Please stop asking me when the AI bubble will pop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
23:37:45 UTC
08:37:45 KST

People, including on this staff, keep asking me with varying degrees of excitement or trepidation when the AI bubble will burst. I’ll tell you what I tell them: If I knew that, I would make a life-changing bet on the market, levered up as far as I could, and then, after I made my money, go retire on a beach somewhere. Maybe run a cat sanctuary, who knows.
Please stop asking me when the AI bubble will pop
I’m getting some real mixed messages here, boys!
I’m getting some real mixed messages here, boys!
What I can tell you is that I read with interest a story in Bloomberg this morning: “Wall Street CEOs, Big Money Managers Divided Over AI Risks.” The story itself is a roundup of stuff said at the 2026 Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit in Hong Kong. Here’s what caught my attention: The CEO of Pacific Investment Management Co. — that’s PIMCO, the legendary bond firm — told listeners that there’s going to be a downturn in the AI market “and then things are going to break.”
“What we don’t know is how pricing and economics will evolve.”
The astronomically expensive AI buildout has swamped debt markets — making it harder to raise cash. But there’s still more debt coming, and people still want to buy it. For instance, Meta drew $58 billion in orders for a bond offering that’s expected to be $15 billion to $20 billion, Bloomberg reported today. Oracle said Monday it would need another $20 billion in bonds, on top of its existing steep commitments. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, is selling €6 billion (or about $6.7 billion) of bonds. Even Microsoft recently sold bonds, for the first time in a decade — $25 billion of them.
The PIMCO CEO — his name is Emmanuel Roman, but his job is what matters here — has estimated that the AI buildout could create $2 trillion in financing needs over the next five years. The entire total US bond market is about $12 trillion.
I am harping on PIMCO because it has been instrumental in the AI trade. It was among the group of financiers that did the first CoreWeave chip-based financing in 2023. It made a quick $2 billion in paper gains from $29 billion in Meta bonds, meant to support the AI buildout, last year. It bought $4 billion of SpaceX bonds last month. If PIMCO’s CEO is publicly sounding the alarm about a bubble popping, that’s a big deal — especially since the company just sold a bunch of its AI debt.
It’s not just PIMCO urging caution. Apollo Global Management, which lately had been talking with SpaceX about a $40 billion chip deal, is also warning of AI risk. Apollo president Jim Zelter told analysts today that while he expects society will use “dramatically more computing power in the future” and that AI is improving quickly, there is still significant uncertainty. “What we don’t know is how pricing and economics will evolve.”
The sheer volume of interest on Meta’s bonds suggests we are not at the top of the market. But there have been reports from China that its AI bubble burst some time ago. Meanwhile Wall Street banks were tripping over themselves to finance $63 billion in debt from Anthropic — not even a hyperscaler.
This is what I mean when I say “I don’t know.” I do think, though, that something major — PIMCO’s Roman singled out US rate hikes, war, or a eurozone crisis as potential triggers — could flip this market. We’re not in go-go-go territory now. Maybe that will change; it’s possible Anthropic’s IPO will go blockbuster and it’ll be like when someone rolls up to a party that’s running low on beer with a 24-pack. But as more people are expressing caution — and particularly after the disaster at Situational Awareness — the best part of the party might be over.

EU Court Advisor Warns Google AI Chatbot May Breach Copyright Rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

EU Court Advisor Warns Google AI Chatbot May Breach Copyright Rules 15
			
		 	
				An adviser to the EU's highest court says Google's Gemini may violate publishers' copyright when it reproduces recognizable portions of their articles or circumvents paywalls and other technical protections to generate answers. Reuters reports:  The case before the Luxembourg-based Court of Justice of the European Union pitted Hungarian website operator Like Company against US-based Google's artificial intelligence chatbot Gemini. A ruling against Google, which could force the tech giant to pay fees for the use of such content, could throw a lifeline to online media such as Like Company. They have seen traffic dwindle as news summaries written by AI chatbots like Gemini increasingly replace traditional search engines' results, which include hyperlinks to the media websites.
"When an LLM (large language model)-driven chatbot retrieves a publication from a press publisher's website, reuses that publication to generate an answer, and provides that answer to the user, the press publisher's right may be infringed in certain circumstances," Advocate General Maciej Szpunar said. Gemini's answers fall under the publishers' right of reproduction when chatbots access publications by unlawfully "circumventing paywalls or other technical barriers, or when they reuse "the form of expression of that publication in a recognizable manner," he said.
Copyright rules do not protect the "mere facts" reported by press publications, but "only the specific form of expression," he added. On the other hand, he said, the use of material protected by copyright to train LLMs -- AI systems that use vast amounts of text to generate human-like responses and summarize information -- is "freely permitted under the text and data mining exception." Szpunar said there was no evidence that Google had used the Hungarian publisher's articles to train Gemini. The court, which follows the majority of its advisers' non-binding opinions, will rule in the coming months.  "Google's powerful gatekeeping role in search makes this particularly important. Publishers depend on Google to reach readers, while Google increasingly delivers AI-generated answers directly to users," said Angela Mills Wade, the council's executive director.
"Publishers should not have to choose between search visibility and protecting their rights. Nor should Google's control over access to audiences become leverage to secure publishers' content for AI services," she said.

Anthropic is working on a system to prove AI models’ identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
22:41:03 UTC
07:41:03 KST

Anthropic is working on an open source system to verify which AI model produced a given output, according to a blog post published Tuesday. The system, called FlashProve, is built to provide what researchers call “provable inference” — a cryptographic proof, essentially a mathematical guarantee, that a given output came from a specific model. It’s meant to let users confirm that the answer they received really came from the model they think they’re using.
Similar to cryptographic email signatures that let recipients confirm a message really came from its claimed sender, FlashProve would be robust against impostors attempting to disguise one model as another, even when the impostor is the lab that built and runs the model. In particular, the researchers note that the system could be used to prevent an AI company from secretly swapping in a cheaper model to cut costs, or a more expensive model to inflate its performance results.
FlashProve could also be used to verify claims by third parties that a specific task was done by an advanced model. “A developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model,” the researchers write. “How can a user verify these claims?”
To work, the system requires AI labs to publish a “fingerprint” of each model they release that can later be matched to specific outputs and verified cryptographically. Crucially, the fingerprints don’t reveal a model’s weights, the internal numbers that define how it behaves and which closed-model makers like Anthropic and OpenAI keep private. That means labs could publish the fingerprints without giving up their most valuable asset, enabling the system to work with commercial models, too. The system is also designed to be lightweight, so verification could be performed on a local device.
As part of the announcement, researchers released a detailed technical specification and working code for various elements of the system, which is publicly available under an open source license on GitHub. Research in the system is ongoing, and there are no plans to deploy it at Anthropic or any other lab.
“This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda,” researchers explain in the announcement post. “We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.”

Assyria is Far from Ancient in Esther Elia’s Characterizations of Contemporary ‘Diasporic Deities’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
22:25:26 UTC
07:25:26 KST

Assyria is Far from Ancient in Esther Elia’s Characterizations of Contemporary ‘Diasporic Deities’
Across ancient Mesopotamia, lamassu figures assumed the form of a winged goddess. In the ancient Assyrian Empire, giant bulls or lions with human heads and wings represented the deities, which artisans often carved at a monumental scale to protect cities and palaces. For Albuquerque-based Esther Elia, who is of Assyrian and Irish descent, lamassu are anything but a relic of the distant past. Through sculpture, paintings, and textiles, the artist explores contemporary Assyrian experience through pattern, fashion, and autobiography.
Her solo exhibition, Bazaar Ashuraya at Hecho a Mano, centers around a new collection of acrylic paintings, plus tile mosaics and functional objects. Elia delves into the theme of home, where lamps, garments, and paintings evocative of rugs or tapestries portray vibrant figures, shapes, and objects associated with daily life. Compositions such as “Sharrat Wearing Adidas” and “Esther and Zahra Wearing Farm Rio” playfully nod to contemporary fashion and folk designs.
“The home is where Assyria lives and breathes,” Elia says in a statement. She adds:
The home is where our language is spoken. Even if we speak English or Arabic or Farsi or French or Swedish outside of the home, the home is where Assyrian food is made, where Assyrian customs thrive, and where culture is maintained as well as created—pushed forward. As we mix with diaspora, our clothes, furnishings, and habits reflect the mixing with these new places.
Elia’s sculptures have reached nearly life-size through the use of Mexican tiles on cement board and plywood, with wheels affixed to the bases so they can move around. She coined these her “diasporic deities” because they incorporate materials readily sourced in the Southwest and are designed to be adaptable to different spaces.
Bazaar Ashuraya runs from November 6 to 29 in Santa Fe, and the artist was recently announced as a 2027 resident of the John Michael Kohler Art Center and Kohler Co.’s Arts/Industry program. See more on Elia’s Instagram.

Data centers are turning to old jet engines as the wait for power grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
22:19:53 UTC
07:19:53 KST

Stuck in years-long lines for grid connections and new turbines, some AI data centers are making their own electricity with converted jet engines, the New York Times reported Tuesday.
The engines, pulled from retired aircraft and rebuilt to burn natural gas, aren’t anyone’s idea of a permanent power plant. But they’re another sign of how far power supply has fallen behind the AI buildout.
For companies stuck in those lines, the main draw of converted jet engines is how quickly the engines can be up and running. “It’s all about getting power as fast as possible,” Rystad Energy analyst Audun Martinsen told the Times. With jet-powered units, “they can have a data center running in 24 months,” he said.
Hooking up 100 megawatts to the grid in Northern Virginia, by comparison, takes about seven years, according to the International Energy Agency. Most power capacity is expected to come on by 2031, an executive at Mitsubishi Power, one of the world’s top makers of power generation equipment, told Bloomberg last week.
In some cases, these delays are already costing some data center operators business. Last month, Microsoft pulled out as the anchor customer for Nscale’s data center in Loughton, England, after the local utility said it couldn’t deliver enough power until the early to mid-2030s.
Elon Musk’s xAI is among the companies already using the engines, having installed eight converted jet-engine turbines in Mississippi to help power its Colossus 2 data center in Memphis, the Times reported, citing state permits and satellite imagery. The units come from ProEnergy, which rebuilds a GE engine commonly found on Boeing jets.
In 2025, OpenAI followed Musk’s lead with gas turbines at its first Stargate site in Abilene, Texas. Crusoe, a Denver-based startup that builds AI data centers, is constructing that Abilene campus and ordered 13 of ProEnergy’s converted units in April.
In September, Crusoe walked away from a $1.25 billion deal to buy 29 natural gas turbines from Boom Supersonic, a startup developing a supersonic passenger jet that has also begun selling a version of that jet’s engine as a power plant for data centers. A Crusoe spokesperson told TechCrunch at the time that the company still plans to use turbines.
Currently the Trump administration is adding to the pressure by encouraging data centers to generate their own electricity.
Converted jet engines come with trade-offs, though: They’re less efficient and pollute more than turbines designed for conventional gas plants, and it takes more of them to make the same amount of power, according to the Times. That may ultimately make converted jet engines a short-term play with some experts saying that efficiency and environmental concerns may grow in importance in a year or two.

Valve is making changes to deal with a ‘significant increase’ in Steam game submissions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
22:17:34 UTC
07:17:34 KST

In a new post today, Valve acknowledged that it’s seen “a significant increase in submissions for store and page review in recent months” and says it’s “running a little behind” by taking “up to 12 business days” for reviews instead of the typical 3-5 days.
Valve is making changes to deal with a ‘significant increase’ in Steam game submissions
Valve admits that it’s now taking ‘up to 12 business days’ to review games.
Indie developers have recently expressed frustrations over lengthy approval times for Steam games, even causing some games to miss planned launch dates. Valve says that “much” of the delay is having to re-review games, so it’s making some changes to the release checklist for developers to hopefully “cut down on re-reviews for basic functional issues.”
The changes include requiring developers to run games through Steam for at least five minutes. “Believe it or not, sometimes we review builds that have not ever been played through Steam,” Valve says. “This means that even if a game runs smoothly when a dev launches their executable directly, they might have missed basic steps that would impact a user installing and playing via Steam.”
Other requirements include making sure that achievements are ready and confirming any required common redistributables, like DirectX or Visual C++, that Steam may need to install.
Valve also says more improvements are in the works for the build review process.

Binance says hackers used fake job interviews and an internal AI tool to pull off the $6.3 billion heist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
22:05:10 UTC
07:05:10 KST

The largest crypto theft to date was pulled off by combining some well-known hacking techniques over the course of a few months, according to Binance. A postmortem from the company says the process started in June with one developer downloading a tampered installer apparently spread by a malicious Google ad, exposing details about the engineers and how they work. Then, in September, another engineer was targeted by someone pretending to be interested in hiring them; that person set up a series of calls and multiple rounds of interviews, shared social media pages to build trust, and eventually prompted them to download a fake interview assignment that was actually malware.
Binance says hackers used fake job interviews and an internal AI tool to pull off the $6.3 billion heist
A North Korean hacking unit reportedly started its break-in with a search engine ad that served up a malware download.
Binance claims that its security teams did detect the first installation of malware in June, and replaced the worker’s device, but that its security tools didn’t detect the second attack that deleted the pyenv executable and replaced it with a malicious version that gave them backdoor access:
The malware employed sophisticated obfuscation and evasion techniques, including replacing a legitimate development tool component with a malicious version to execute commands and establish communication with an attacker-controlled external server. The 0-day malware was not detected by the endpoint security protection tools at the time. The attacker also took steps to conceal the malicious activity and remove traces of the compromise, making detection and subsequent investigation more challenging.
By October 20th, the story goes, the attackers, whom the FBI has identified as a North Korean unit dubbed “TraderTraitor,” used Binance’s own internal AI tool to gain control over wallets for the first engineer compromised in June, as well as a third employee, before logging into the third employee’s computer on October 29th and launching their attack.
The postmortem also goes into why Binance wasn’t able to stop the transactions that occurred nearly two hours after the first unauthorized transfers, saying that “Because the hot wallet used Multi-Party Computation (MPC), there was no single private key that could be used to immediately revoke the malicious EIP-7702 authorizations.” Binance says that it has prevented 57 suspected North Korea-linked cyber threat cases, and CEO Richard Teng writes that no user is bearing the loss, with about $2.85 billion in stolen assets frozen or intercepted: “At this moment, 98% of impacted tokens had been replenished; we’re completing the remaining 2%. Withdrawals have broadly resumed.”
What’s less clear is why this particular attack worked — the danger of job interviews that ask people to download and execute code on machines with access to employer material has been warned about for years, and there’s little detail on the “internal AI tool” that was used by the attackers and why it was able to help them in the first place.

The Internals of PostgreSQL
PostgreSQL is a well-designed, open-source multi-purpose relational database system which is widely used throughout the world.
It is one huge system with the integrated subsystems, each of which has a particular complex feature and works cooperatively with each other. Although understanding of the internal mechanism is crucial for both administration and integration using PostgreSQL, its hugeness and complexity make it difficult.
The main purposes of this documentation are to explain how each subsystem works, and to provide the whole picture of PostgreSQL.
This documentation covers versions 19-beta (excluding the new buffer page lock mechanism) and earlier.
Some academic papers have referred to this documentation. The Chinese version of this documentation was published in June 2019.
This documentation was first published on 26 September 2015.
- Chapter 1. Database Cluster, Databases and Tables
- Chapter 2. Process and Memory Architecture
- Chapter 3. Query Processing
- Chapter 4. Foreign Data Wrappers (FDW)
- Chapter 5. Concurrency Control
- Chapter 6. VACUUM Processing
- Chapter 7. Heap Only Tuple (HOT) and Index-Only Scans
- Chapter 8. Buffer Manager
- Chapter 9. Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
- Chapter 10. Online Backup and Point-In-Time Recovery (PITR)
- Chapter 11. Streaming Replication
- Chapter 12. Logical Replication (Beta Version)
Author
Hironobu SUZUKI
I am a software programmer/engineer, the author of:
I graduated from graduate school in information engineering (M.S. in Information Engineering), have worked for several companies as a software developer and technical manager/director. I published seven books in the fields of database and system integration (4 PostgreSQL books and 3 MySQL books). In June 2019, the Chinese book of this documentation was published.
As a director of the Japan PostgreSQL Users Group (2010-2016), I organized the largest (non-commercial) technical seminar/lecture on PostgreSQL in Japan for more than six years, and also served as the program committee chair of the Japan PostgreSQL Conference in 2013 and as a member in 2008 and 2009.
In June 2022, my interview article was published in “PostgreSQL person of the week”.

Ted Schlein’s Ballistic Ventures seeks $490M for new funds amid AI-driven cybersecurity boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
21:43:08 UTC
06:43:08 KST

Ballistic Ventures, the cybersecurity-focused venture capital firm co-founded by former Kleiner Perkins partner Ted Schlein (pictured above, second from the right), is seeking to raise $490 million across two new funds, TechCrunch has learned through regulatory filings.
The San Francisco-based VC firm filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission this week to raise $360 million for its third flagship fund, matching the size of its previous fund raised in 2024, and another $130 million for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund B. Neither fund had recorded any sales at the time of filing.
The fundraising plans come as the growing use of artificial intelligence has raised concerns about more sophisticated cyberattacks. The rise of AI agents has also created new opportunities for cybersecurity startups and the venture capital firms backing them.
Founded in late 2021, Ballistic Ventures’ founding team includes Schlein, former AT&T Cybersecurity president Barmak Meftah, and Roger Thornton, who co-founded security companies Fortify Software and AlienVault. The firm has backed companies, including Talon Cyber Security, acquired by Palo Alto Networks, and Pangea, bought by CrowdStrike, alongside startups such as Armadin, GetReal, Nudge Security, and Oligo Security.
Ballistic’s ties to storied venture capital firm Kleiner Perkins, where Schlein spent more than two decades, help set it apart from rivals, a cybersecurity investor at another VC firm told TechCrunch. Its investment strategy, however, is similar to those of other cybersecurity-focused investors, including Forgepoint Capital and Ten Eleven Ventures, the person said.
In 2022, Ballistic announced its $300 million debut fund and raised another $360 million for its second flagship fund two years later. It also raised about $130 million for a separate vehicle called Ballistic Ventures Fund A, per PitchBook data. The new Fund B is targeting a similar amount.
U.S. cybersecurity startups raised $11.5 billion in 2025, the highest since 2022, a recent report by JPMorgan Chase said, citing PitchBook data. AI-enabled companies accounted for about 72% of U.S. cybersecurity venture deals through May this year, compared with 36% in 2019, the report said.
Separately, Microsoft, in its annual Digital Defense Report released last month, warned that hackers are increasingly using AI for activities ranging from phishing and social engineering to malware development. The technology is allowing attackers to operate faster and at greater scale, even as many of their underlying techniques remain unchanged.
Ballistic Ventures declined to comment on its fundraising plans.

Title:The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:This book provides a compact, derivation-oriented introduction to the mathematical foundations of modern generative artificial intelligence. Rather than surveying every recent architecture or implementation detail, it develops a coherent route through the ideas connecting major families of generative models, from PCA, probabilistic PCA, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models to normalising flows, autoregressive factorisations, GANs, Wasserstein GANs, and energy-based models. The aim is to make the structure of generative modelling more accessible without removing the mathematical substance needed to understand how these models are derived and related. The book is intended as a foundation-building primer for mathematically curious researchers, practitioners, and students.

Title:The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:This book provides a compact, derivation-oriented introduction to the mathematical foundations of modern generative artificial intelligence. Rather than surveying every recent architecture or implementation detail, it develops a coherent route through the ideas connecting major families of generative models, from PCA, probabilistic PCA, variational autoencoders, and diffusion models to normalising flows, autoregressive factorisations, GANs, Wasserstein GANs, and energy-based models. The aim is to make the structure of generative modelling more accessible without removing the mathematical substance needed to understand how these models are derived and related. The book is intended as a foundation-building primer for mathematically curious researchers, practitioners, and students.

Safari introduces Adaptive Dark Mode in 27.3
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
21:39:05 UTC
06:39:05 KST

Introducing Adaptive Dark Mode
We’re excited to announce Adaptive Dark Mode in Safari 27.3 beta. When enabled by a user, Safari adapts light websites and presents them as dark.
In the spring of 2019, Safari 12.1 became the first browser to support dark mode on the web. A lot of people love using dark mode, but not every website has a dark version. Almost 40% of web page loads are from users in dark mode, and yet only 10% of page loads support it. If you love dark mode, you’ve probably hit a site that felt particularly bright. Adaptive Dark Mode is designed to close that gap, providing a consistent dark experience across the web.
You can try it today in Safari 27.3 beta. To enable, first make sure your system appearance is set to dark. Then browse to a website with a bright background. Safari will offer a preview of Adaptive Dark Mode. Tap ‘Try’.
For websites that signal support of dark mode with <meta name="color-scheme" content="light dark"> in HTML or color-scheme: light dark in CSS, Adaptive Dark Mode does not change a thing. For the rest of the web, it quickly analyzes the page, looking at colors and estimating whether it’s predominantly light or dark. If the page generally has a dark background with light text, nothing is changed. When a page has a light appearance, Adaptive Dark Mode adapts the page to be dark.
How does Adaptive Dark Mode work?
At the core of Adaptive Dark Mode is the transformation of color. Sometimes colors are simply decorative, while other times they have semantic meaning. Adaptive Dark Mode determines when to invert colors so elements remain visible or when to leave colors unchanged.
While creating Adaptive Dark Mode, we developed a color matrix to invert the luminosity of colors while preserving hue. It’s used to make light backgrounds dark, and dark text light. When transforming text color, Adaptive Dark Mode aims for sufficient contrast as defined by the WCAG 4.5:1 contrast ratio. Light CSS gradients are also transformed to dark.
Adaptive Dark Mode makes careful judgments so transformed content looks good and stays usable: buttons have contrast against backgrounds, text is visible over images, and hover menus look clear.
It takes the same care with images. Most are left unchanged, preserving their integrity. But many icons and logos can lose contrast when the background color behind them is inverted. So Adaptive Dark Mode inspects SVG images and transforms colors when needed. For bitmap images, it analyzes the pixel histograms and inverts simple black-and-white logos.
Effects like masks and mix-blend-mode can create undesirable results on an element whose colors have been transformed, so in some cases Adaptive Dark Mode turns such effects off. Also, <canvas> content is left unchanged, since canvases contain a wide range of content that’s hard to predict.
It’s precisely because Adaptive Dark Mode is happening deep within the WebKit browser engine that we are able to find creative ways to solve the most complex challenges, apply the transformations with great speed and power efficiency, all while rigorously protecting user privacy.
Making your site work even better
In general, a web page will work well with Adaptive Dark Mode if it follows good modern web development practices.
If your site still uses older techniques, small updates can help. For logos and icons, swap bitmap images for SVG. Use solid or gradient colors in CSS instead of tiled background images. Replace image sprites with modern CSS for rounded corners, shadows, and button states. Create content images with transparent backgrounds instead of baking the page background color into the image. Add padding to containers to prevent crowding.
Perhaps you want a specific dark mode experience for a certain portion of the page. Apply color-scheme: light dark to the relevant element and add your own dark styles.
Building your own dark mode
For complete control over how your site looks in dark mode, add full support. It’s a terrific time to do so. It’s never been easier.
All the web technology needed to fully support dark mode is widely available today, including:
Newer CSS functions like color-mix() and contrast-color(), plus popular techniques for organizing design systems with CSS variables provide additional options and flexibility.
Be sure to declare dark mode support using the color-scheme meta tag in your HTML head and/or by setting the color-scheme property on :root or body in your CSS. Don’t wait to inject this information later via JavaScript. This best practice helps ensure your site is rendered correctly as fast as possible.
Using the “light only” color scheme
If you would like your web app or website to not be transformed by Adaptive Dark Mode, you can communicate this using color-scheme. The HTML <meta name="color-scheme" content="light only"> tag lets browsers know that 1) this page supports light mode and 2) should only be displayed in light mode. The color-scheme: light only rule does the same thing, but with the flexibility of CSS, allowing you to just target specific elements on the page — or of course, you can target the whole page with :root { }. (Note: the ‘only’ keyword is not supported in Safari 27.3 beta 1. Check back as Adaptive Dark Mode evolves through the beta process.)
Protecting user privacy
Apple firmly believes user privacy is a fundamental human right. If websites could detect when a user has enabled Adaptive Dark Mode, that would increase the amount of fingerprintable information and weaken privacy protections against trackers.
As a result, Safari prevents websites from detecting when Adaptive Dark Mode has been applied. JavaScript that queries CSS colors will get the original authored colors, not the transformed ones. Any images drawn into canvas render in their original form.
Feedback
If you manage a website or web app, and would like to discuss how Adaptive Dark Mode is adapting your project, feel free to reach out at web-evangelist@apple.com.
If you try out Adaptive Dark Mode as a user, and find a site that does not work well, we’d love for you to file a report with Feedback Assistant. (Learn more about filing Feedback).

Here’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
21:25:24 UTC
06:25:24 KST

It’s impossible to paint a full picture of what Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 will be right now. The watchOS 27.3 developer beta just dropped earlier this afternoon, and these features are meant to be lived with in day-to-day life. We’re definitely going to do that over the next few weeks at The Verge. That said, here are some initial impressions.
Here’s what it’s like to use Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch
The watchOS 27.3 beta adds Live Rewind and Siri Recap to the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4.
What’s newly available today is Live Rewind and Siri Recap. The former lets you see a transcript of the last 15 seconds, while the latter provides high-level summaries of your conversations. (The other two Audio Intelligence features have been available for the last few weeks. I wrote about those in my Series 12 review.) And as always, this is the developer beta. These features could still change quite a bit before a final version arrives for the public.
The first thing I noticed is that these features are not turned on by default. I wasn’t expecting anything different, but it’s worth remembering that these features don’t automatically turn every Apple Watch into a surveillance device. Audio Intelligence requires the latest Apple Watch hardware, a compatible version of iOS (so in this case, the iOS 27.3 developer beta), and someone has to actively choose to enable these features. You can download the beta and double-press the crown to initiate a Live Rewind. It won’t do anything. You must opt in via your iPhone’s Watch app. Same goes for Siri Recap. Enabling Live Rewind also requires an initial microphone calibration with your phone.
Privacy-wise, Apple has publicly available support documentation about its approach to these features. I’m not weighing in on how well it executes them in this hands-on. But Apple has pretty clear messaging in the onboarding process. There are quite a few customization options for when Siri Recap is active. You can get pretty granular. For example, you can have Siri Recap on only at the office during weekdays from 1PM to 4PM if that’s when you have meetings. This is hard to convey to bystanders, and I think ethical use should come with an in-person heads-up to the people you frequently interact with. (Hello, fellow Verge writers and editors.)
Live Rewind, so far, has worked as described — with the heavy caveat that I’ve only tested it in my quiet home office with my spouse. Even so, it takes a hot second to learn the timing of a double press. My spouse noticed the audible chime signaling the feature is in use, though they didn’t notice the animation. I’ll have to see how this fares in louder environments. Siri accurately captured our attempts to get my cat to roll over, though in subsequent tests, it misheard a word or two.
I’m more hesitant to comment on Siri Recap. It’s not just because I haven’t had many organic, lengthy spoken conversations yet since downloading the beta. (Siri did not deem my brief conversation with my spouse as worthy enough for recapping.) But I won’t really get a sense for how this feature feels until I’ve tested it in a wide variety of scenarios. Will it work if I talk to myself aloud? How well does it filter out gossip? How will this change how people speak to me? That’ll be the true test of this feature and Apple’s bystander privacy claims.
My first Siri Recap was for an editorial planning meeting for a story I’m working on. It was decent at identifying different topics discussed, and I was impressed that it stripped out some sensitive information. Any outsider looking at these notes would be terribly confused. Ironically, it meant that this summary wasn’t the most useful for my job.
What I will say is that I’ve been testing the Amazon Bee Frontier for the past few weeks. In the little time I’ve spent with the watchOS 27.3 beta, the differences between Audio Intelligence and the Bee are very clear. The latter has more of what I’d call an AI-forward presence. Bee, for example, offers insights about the emotional tone of a conversation. I’ve also found that the AI can be a bit judgy about insights and takeaways. Live Rewind is just a straight transcript. Apple’s said publicly that Siri Recap is meant to be highly factual notes to jog a person’s memory. That rings true based on my first one. And, as far as I can tell, there is no commerce angle for Siri Recaps, whereas Bee has an Amazon integration that surfaces buying suggestions based on conversations.
In any case, I’ll be diving deep into these features in the days to come. Let us know in the comments what you’re most curious about.
