$20 Million In Fines And Still Vizio Smart TVs Opt Out Of Spying Option Does Nothing
There’s A Quote From Leftist Gamer Memes (Not Final Fantasy Tactics) Which Seems Applicable
We’ve already heard the reports about the behaviour of LG TVs as well as the absolute denials from them about what researchers found, now new research has been published about the behaviour of some of their competitors. As you should expect, that news is not good. Researchers at Northeastern University conducted 5,943 experiments across twelve commercial smart TVs to see just what opting out of automatic content recognition monitoring options did.
Instead of trying to determine what ACR data was being sent to IP addresses known to be associated with advertisers and personal data trackers they instead monitored the effect on the traffic generated by a TV when it was opted out of optional data harvesting. Devices using webOS, Fire OS, Sony Google TV, and VIDAA OS did indeed stop sending traffic when requested to using the options in the menu, only 60% of the Samsung Tizen smart TVs showed decreased or no traffic.
The big winner was Vizio, where there was no change at all in traffic when the option to disable any and all tracking was enabled. They simply carried on as if you had agreed to share all your data. Again, the researchers didn’t attempt to read the traffic, they only monitored it’s volume and destinations. Vizio was fined $2.2 million by the FTC in 2017 for not informing customers of their TV’s spying habits which resulted in a $17 million lawsuit which Vizio lost. It would seem that the income they rake in from spying outweighs the cost of being caught.
Also, before you congratulate yourself on using a TV running VIDAA, such as Hisense and Toshiba, you should know that traffic from the ACR data they collect is sent completely and totally unencrpyted and contains things which should not be.
We find that the advertised ACR opt-out fully suppresses ACR-attributable traffic on only four operating systems; on Samsung Tizen traffic consistent with ACR activity persists in more than 60% of evaluated scenarios, and on Vizio SmartCast a content correlated endpoint hosted on Amazon Kinesis continues to receive traffic in 100% of opted-out scenarios.

Casio announced a new addition to its Casiotone line of portable electronic keyboards with a feature that could help aspiring musicians master skills like rhythm and timing without the frustrations or discouragement of hitting the wrong note.
You can’t hit a wrong note when playing along with songs on Casio’s new keyboard
The $400 CT-FS1 features Casio’s Feel Sync technology that helps inexperienced musicians hit only the right notes.
The Casiotone CT-FS1 is available now for $399.99 in a monochromatic black or white version where even the 61 touch-responsive keys are all the same color. It can run on AA batteries or a power adapter but at just under 10 pounds in weight it’s definitely not the smallest of portable keyboards. Through the app you can import a song file which is analyzed by an algorithm before playing through the keyboard. As you play along with the song the keyboard will only produce notes that match the song’s harmony, no matter what keys you press. You’re still responsible for timing and matching the song’s rhythm, but the keyboard takes care of everything else so you can work on developing your creative expression without being self-conscious about it sounding awful.
The CT-FS1 can be played like a standard keyboard without the Feel Sync assistance, but because it’s long enough to accommodate two musicians, you can also split the keyboard into two zones. Crypto giant Binance says North Korean hackers used fake social media profiles and the lure of a potential job offer as part of a months-long scheme aimed at tricking an employee into downloading malicious software onto their laptop.
Researchers have repeatedly warned about long-running social engineering attacks that can go on for months.
This latest attack allowed the hackers to patiently worm their way into Binance’s systems to steal a record $6.3 billion in crypto last week, the company has now confirmed. The hack, disclosed in an updated statement posted on X on Tuesday, prompted the world’s largest crypto exchange to suspend customer withdrawals across its network.
The FBI and blockchain investigators have blamed North Korea for the heist. The country has been long accused of carrying out massive cryptocurrency thefts in recent years to fund its internationally sanctioned nuclear weapons program.
In its latest statement, Binance said that North Korean hackers, posing as recruiters hiring for a job, contacted a software engineer who works on wallets at the company. Following two interviews with the purported company, the engineer was instructed to download an apparent coding assignment as part of the interview process. When opened, the assignment contained malicious code that compromised the engineer’s work-issued laptop. Binance said its security tools did not detect the malware.
That foothold in Binance’s network allowed the hackers to access an internal tool capable of taking over the work computers of two other engineers on the wallet team. One of those engineers had unwittingly downloaded a tampered app containing password-stealing malware months earlier after searching for the software in search engine results. While Binance replaced that compromised engineer’s laptop, the hackers used the engineer’s stolen credentials to break into the computer of a third engineer, whose job allowed them access to systems capable of controlling billions of dollars in crypto.
Binance said the attack “should not have happened,” and that it had improved its network security following the theft.
The hack underscores an ongoing tactic in the North Korean regime’s repertoire of attacks targeting the crypto industry and high-net worth individuals. Researchers have warned for years that North Korean hackers pose as venture capitalists, investors, and recruiters using dossiers of stolen American identities to trick employees into granting access to their systems.
These attacks are widely known across the crypto industry and have been the subject of repeated warnings from the U.S. government and cybersecurity giants in recent years. Some half of all intrusions at U.S. tech companies last year were attributed to North Koreans posing as remote IT workers and fake recruiters.
By Binance’s own account, the company faced at least 57 suspected attacks from North Korea, which it said reflect the “persistent threat posed by state-sponsored actors targeting the cryptocurrency industry.”
But how the hackers were able to convince the engineer into downloading malware given the highly publicized threat, and bypass security weaknesses in Binance’s own network, will likely be the focus of investigators’ attention.
While the case exposes how North Korean hackers use social engineering, such as offers of employment, to trick employees into granting access to their systems, it’s ultimately the responsibility of the company to ensure its systems cannot run unauthorized or untrusted software that could cause a compromise.
A Binance spokesperson referred to the company’s public statement but declined to answer TechCrunch’s questions on the record about the incident. Those questions included how Binance prevents unauthorized or malicious code from running on its employees’ laptops, if at all, and whether any third parties had performed cybersecurity audits of Binance’s network prior to the hack.
The company said it would bring in cybersecurity experts to review the incident and has put new security measures in place to prevent a repeat incident.
The heist remains the largest theft of crypto in history.
Updated to remove name of Binance spokesperson in thirteenth paragraph.

This Election Day, remember which party ran against EVs and tethered us all to the gas pump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
19:44:46 UTC
04:44:46 KST

It’s the midterms! Here’s a fun fact for you as you head to the polls: Gas prices today are the highest ever recorded for a US Election Day.
This Election Day, remember which party ran against EVs and tethered us all to the gas pump
Donald Trump and congressional Republicans spent years waging a culture war against EVs. Now, record gas prices and a foreign war are leaving voters stuck footing the bill at the pump.
The national average for a gallon of gasoline is $4.12 and $6.28 for a gallon of diesel, according to GasBuddy. Meanwhile, the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, which is maintained by the US Department of Energy as a safeguard during energy crises, is down to 282.2 million barrels of crude, the lowest level in 44 years.
Gas prices, along with other essential cost-of-living items, are certainly top of mind for many voters this election cycle. And perhaps many will also remember which political party ran on a campaign message of ending the fictional “EV mandate” and “drill, baby, drill.”
For the past two years, Donald Trump and congressional Republicans have made gutting EV incentives, freezing charging infrastructure funding, and rolling back fuel economy standards a hallmark of their tenure in power. As a result, EV sales plummeted in the US, ensuring that Americans would stay indefinitely shackled to fossil fuels for years to come. For Trump, it was fulfilling a promise he made during the 2024 campaign. And for his donors from the oil and gas industry, it was money well spent.
Most voters might not have cared that much. After all, skepticism toward EVs was already high, driven by premium prices and lingering charging anxiety. But when Trump went to war with Iran, the resulting surge in gas prices sent Americans scrambling for cheaper ways to get around. Many turned to hybrid and electric vehicles as a solution — only to find vehicle prices were still higher than average, with no federal incentive to help defray the costs. Dealerships saw a surge of foot traffic from drivers who were skeptical of battery-powered cars, now desperate for anything that ran on a plug or a hybrid motor.
While automakers had made strides toward cheaper EVs, the average transaction price still hovered well over $50,000. But the incentive that once helped close that gap — the $7,500 federal clean vehicle tax credit, applied instantly at the point of sale — was gone. The subsidies had been systematically dismantled or left to lapse under the banner of fiscal discipline and anti-green populism.
Here is the real irony of this election. Republicans spent years painting electric cars as an out-of-touch, liberal fad, doing everything they could to kill tax credits and charging programs. They rolled back fuel economy standards that would have forced automakers to build more fuel-efficient powertrains, claiming they were saving everyday drivers from expensive technology they didn’t want.
Instead, they took away an important tool that could have protected family budgets from a global energy crisis. Electricity is made right here at home; its price doesn’t spike every time conflict breaks out in the Middle East. But because Republicans treated EVs like a partisan culture war, millions of Americans are stuck standing at the pump, watching the price roll higher.
Even if Democrats win back Congress, don’t expect them to bring back the Biden-era EV tax credits. The political fight over what kind of car people drive is probably stuck. At the same time, major car companies are backing Trump’s push in court to roll back strict fuel-economy rules. Electric cars aren’t disappearing, but they now have to stand on their own two feet. Companies like General Motors and Ford do have plans to make them more affordable, as long as the government keeps blocking cheap Chinese models from entering the market.
In the end, Trump won his culture war against the electric car. Automakers retreated, subsidies vanished, and the traditional combustion engine was saved from the bureaucrats. But victories have price tags. And as voters step into the booth with a $4 gallon of gas on their minds, they might finally realize what was traded away: the simple freedom to drive past the pump and never look back.

AI inference startup Fal doubles its valuation to $16B as demand surges

Fal, a San Francisco-based startup that hosts and runs AI video, image, and audio models, has raised $1.3 billion in its latest funding round led by Bessemer Venture Partners, with participation from Nvidia, Sound Ventures, and T. Rowe Price. The deal values Fal at $16 billion, double its $8 billion valuation in April, Bloomberg reported.
The startup announced its Series E and F rounds at the same time, noting that a combined $1.65 billion was raised across both. (Sequoia led the earlier round.)
The latest round (Series F) comes amid soaring demand for inference services, the process of running an AI model that’s already been trained to generate outputs, particularly from customers relying on open source models. Fal surpassed $800 million in annualized revenue earlier this year, Bloomberg’s report noted.
Companies providing inference services, including Baseten, Fireworks AI, and Modal, have also been growing rapidly and raising large funding rounds at higher valuations. But their gross margins remain thin because of the high cost of buying or leasing compute, according to several people familiar with inference companies’ financials.
Fal was co-founded in 2021 by Burkay Gur, a former Coinbase machine learning leader and Oracle engineer, and Gorkem Yurtseven, who was previously a developer at Amazon.

Preparing for the Flipper One Kickstarter and opening pre-orders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
19:32:13 UTC
04:32:13 KST

FLIPPER ONE
Open Linux computer based on a powerful ARM processor. Network multi-tool — built-in Wi-Fi 6E and Gigabit Ethernet. Expandable via M.2 modules: 5G cellular modem, SDR radio and more.
Follow progress at the Developer Portal >>
OPEN LINUX PLATFORM
Flipper One runs on completely open-source Linux firmware with a mainline kernel. This means ultimate compatibility with bleeding-edge kernel versions, free from vendor-specific BSP limitations and binary blobs. Our goal is to create a fully upstream-supported ARM computer that never becomes outdated, and a well-documented platform giving the community maximum freedom to customize:
- Full mainline Linux kernel support
- No binary blobs
- No vendor-locked BSP
We have partnered with the Collabora team, who are actively working on bringing the RK3576 SoC into the mainline kernel, to make Flipper One fully upstream-supported and free from binary blobs. Read Collabora blog post
CO-PROCESSOR ARCHITECTURE
Two independent processors work together in parallel, each controlling different sub-systems of Flipper One. 
This architecture allows you to control the Linux sub-system directly from the built-in LCD display, without losing access to the device even when the Linux kernel is not yet ready or turned off.
Why 2 processors?
- Low-power MCU (Raspberry Pi RP2350) — an energy-efficient microcontroller responsible for core device control. It drives the LCD display, physical buttons, and status LEDs. It manages the power sub-system and controls the Linux OS boot parameters when the Linux sub-system is off. More about MCU Firmware >>
- High-performance CPU (Rockchip RK3576) — a powerful 8-core ARM system-on-chip that runs the Linux operating system. It executes user applications, controls all networking interfaces such as Wi-Fi and Ethernet, and manages high-speed peripherals including USB3 and PCIe. It also integrates an NPU for AI acceleration and a GPU for graphics output via HDMI and DisplayPort. More about Linux sub-system >>
ONE CABLE FOR EVERYTHING
Get SSH access and charge the device via a single USB cable! No extra adapters needed for Linux console access or powering the device — Flipper One can simultaneously emulate a virtual network adapter, a serial adapter (COM port), and a mass-storage device.
No drivers required on macOS, Linux, Windows, iOS, or Android.
NETWORK MULTI‑TOOL
Multi-WAN network toolkit — connect up to 5 uplinks. Configure dynamic routing, failover, load balancing, and firewall rules. Use it simultaneously as a Wi‑Fi hotspot and client. Tunnel traffic through a VPN and multiple gateways.
NETWORK SCANNER
Analyze wired and wireless IP networks. Flipper One helps you map network topology, discover active hosts, and scan for open ports and services. It can also act as a passive sensor to detect network attacks and report anomalies.
POWER METER
The power consumption meter works like a wattmeter, showing in real time how much power the entire system uses, including the CPU and peripherals. It helps you understand what is happening under the hood: whether the system is idle or actively working.
M.2 MODULES
The core idea of Flipper One is an expandable hardware platform. Create your own specialized tool with a high-speed M.2 expansion module that installs inside the device, under the back plate. It supports almost any type of module — cellular or satellite modems, SDR modules, AI accelerators, SSDs (NVMe or SATA), and Wi-Fi cards via adapters.
M.2 tech specs
Read full M.2 Port specification in docs.
- M.2 type: Key-B
- Supported sizes: 2230 (via extender), 2242, 3042, 3052
- Supported thickness: up to D3 (double-sided modules)
- Interfaces: PCIe 2.1 ×1 / USB 2.0 / USB 3.1 / SATA3 / SIM card + eSIM
- Extra interfaces: Serial Audio / UART / I²C
Open source mounting system
All mechanical parts for module mounting are completely open source. You can design your own antennas, cooling system, and mounting solutions for additional accessories.
GPIO MODULES
DIY modules can be connected via the GPIO connector using standard 2.54 mm pin headers. To make the assembled device easier to carry around, the GPIO module is positioned along the device body and can be covered with a protective cover.
Check out GPIO technical specification and examples of GPIO modules.
Desktop Mode
Connect Flipper One to an external display with a single USB-C cable for a full desktop experience. Support for DisplayPort Alt Mode allows one cable to deliver power, transmit video, and connect USB peripherals such as a keyboard and mouse simultaneously.
Satellite NTN Modem
Satellite modem
NTN (Non-Terrestrial Networks) — is a satellite communication technology, a low-speed connection designed for IoT devices, standardized by 3GPP as part of the 5G and LTE specifications. It uses the standard cellular stack, including SIM/eSIM authentication, roaming, and regular IP traffic.
We want to add NTN satellite connectivity support to Flipper One to help popularize this technology and give engineers and enthusiasts a chance to work with real satellite infrastructure. 
To make this happen, we're looking for a partner company like Skylo that's ready to work with us to add support for their satellite network to our eSIM module and help us choose a specific NTN M.2 module that we can officially support. 
Read more on the Modules → Satellite modem page.
Built-in Advanced Wi-Fi Chip
Built-in Wi-Fi Chip
We want to build the most versatile integrated Wi-Fi into Flipper One — it needs to support all the features required for Wi-Fi network analysis, including monitor mode and packet injection. For now, we've settled on the popular Mediatek MT7921U chipset. It's modern enough, supports three frequency bands, and ticks just about every box. We're actively testing this chip right now and we'd love you to join in.
Why MT7921AUN?
The same chipset is used in the popular ALFA AWUS036AXML adapter, and there's a sizeable community around the open-source MT7921U driver. The main strengths of this chipset:
- Modern Wi-Fi 6E: 802.11ax, 2x2 MIMO
- Frequencies: 2.4 / 5 / 6 GHz bands
- Open mainline Linux driver: mt7921u
- Monitor mode support
- Integrated Bluetooth 5.2
BUILT-IN eSIM
Flipper One has a built-in eSIM chip that comes pre‑provisioned with a Flipper SIM data plan.
To use the eSIM data plan, you need to install a 5G modem in the M.2 slot. You can also switch between the built-in eSIM and a physical SIM card.
What is Flipper SIM?
We're working on an experimental connectivity project for network geeks. Flipper SIM is a universal SIM card for routers, phones, and IoT devices, with advanced features such as always-on connectivity, outage-proof, traffic filtering, and network management tools. We'll share more details soon!

macOS 27 does not support CoreStorage volumes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
19:27:53 UTC
04:27:53 KST

macOS 15 Sequoia had a hard time with CoreStorage – and thus encrypted HFS+ volumes – since it deprecated both technologies and callously crippled some important tools for working with them, but nonetheless it mostly still worked. While I’d often – but not always – have to manually unlock one of my HFS+ volumes – but not the others – at boot, and it also refused to convert some – but not all – volumes from HFS+ to APFS1, keeping me trapped in the situation – it ultimately still worked. I could get at my data and use the volumes more or less normally.
Unfortunately, in macOS 27 that’s no longer the case. Not only does Golden Gate just not support CoreStorage / encrypted HFS+ volumes, out of the box you can’t do anything with them – can’t mount them, can’t convert them to APFS, can’t even erase them. It renders your expensive storage hardware completely useless.
Worse, macOS 27 puts up a misleading dialog, upon boot, saying that macOS 28 (the next version) won’t support these volumes. I have no idea what Apple’s doing or thinking. Maybe it’s all just an embarrassing misunderstanding – the file system team told the notifications team that CoreStorage & encrypted HFS+ support is going away, and typoed the version number as 28 rather than 27?
Details
macOS 27 cannot mount CoreStorage volumes automatically or through any normal means. Worse, Disk Utility can’t mount them even when manually told to – it just fails with the cryptic error:
com.apple.DiskManagement.disenter error 49,153
diskutil mount also fails, this time with an error message that is a blatant lie:
disk27 is a CoreStorage Logical Volume which is locked; use "diskutil coreStorage unlockVolume"
$ diskutil cs unlockVolume BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D
BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D is already unlocked and is attached as disk27
$ diskutil cs list
CoreStorage logical volume groups (1 found)
|
+-- Logical Volume Group 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
=========================================================
Name: Smash
Status: Online
Size: 2000054960128 B (2.0 TB)
Free Space: 0 B (0 B)
|
+-< Physical Volume 1B5A1754-184B-4F17-A797-BF69B4BB627F
| ----------------------------------------------------
| Index: 0
| Disk: disk10s2
| Status: Online
| Size: 2000054960128 B (2.0 TB)
|
+-> Logical Volume Family 376204CD-8048-4962-B05C-72F4FC16B77B
----------------------------------------------------------
Encryption Type: AES-XTS
Encryption Status: Unlocked
Conversion Status: Complete
High Level Queries: Fully Secure
| Passphrase Required
| Accepts New Users
| Has Visible Users
| Has Volume Key
|
+-> Logical Volume BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D
---------------------------------------------------
Disk: disk27
Status: Online
Size (Total): 1999702634496 B (2.0 TB)
Revertible: No
LV Name: Smash
Volume Name: Smash
Content Hint: Apple_HFS
But what’s even worse about this dumpster fire is that macOS 27 can mount these volumes just fine – it’s just that all the normal ways to do it are completely broken.  If you go down to a lower level and run mount_hfs directly, it does work:
$ sudo mkdir -p /Volumes/Smash
$ sudo mount_hfs -o rdonly /dev/disk27 /Volumes/Smash
$ ls /Volumes/Smash
Documents Pictures Scratch space
That said… that -o rdonly parameter… in principle it shouldn’t be required, but I could not get macOS 27 to let me mount any HFS-on-CoreStorage volume as read-write – no matter what I did, it always fails with error “Resource busy” (EBUSY). I spent a lot of time trying to debug this, and could find no evidence of anything having the volume in question open (nothing in lsof etc).
But wait, it gets worse.
macOS 27 can’t even erase the volume.  All the normal tools – diskutil, Disk Utility, etc – fail with that same “Resource busy” error.
Workaround
Thankfully, with the help of Gemini 4 Argon, I did find a workaround. It’s convoluted, but takes only a few steps, thankfully.
First, while if you try to delete the logical volume group it ostensibly fails, it doesn’t completely fail – it does actually delete the logical volume(s) within:
$ diskutil cs delete 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
Started CoreStorage operation
Unmounting Logical Volumes
Destroying Logical Volume Group
Erasing disk10s2
newfs_hfs: cannot create filesystem on /dev/rdisk10s2: Resource busy
Mounting disk
Could not mount disk10s2 after erase
Error: -69832: File system formatter failed
1 💣 $ diskutil cs list
CoreStorage logical volume groups (1 found)
|
+-- Logical Volume Group 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
=========================================================
Name: Smash
Status: Offline
Size: 2000054960128 B (2.0 TB)
Free Space: -none-
|
+-< Physical Volume 1B5A1754-184B-4F17-A797-BF69B4BB627F
----------------------------------------------------
(No properties)
$ diskutil cs delete 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
Started CoreStorage operation
Destroying Logical Volume Group
Error: -69783: Unable to delete the CoreStorage Logical Volume Group
You still can’t destroy it completely, nor can you erase the physical volume yet – the “Resource busy” errors persist. But, the trick is to restart – after that, you can then erase the volume.
So it seems that whatever broken thing is holding the physical volume (or logical volume group) in a ‘busy’ state is tied to the existence of the logical volume(s) therein, and once they’re deleted (and the machine rebooted) the bug stops being triggered.
Call for better workarounds
I’ve glossed over a lot of debugging and attempts I made to save the volume in-place, by either making it work as-is (even if only with e.g. hfsutils) or by converting it to APFS, but neither I nor Gemini 4 Argon could find anything that worked. It’s too late for me – I was forced to just delete all my HFS+ & CoreStorage volumes and rebuild them painstakingly from backups – but if anyone finds a way, I’d love to amend this post, for the benefit of future readers.
- The problem remains the same in macOS 27 – so three major macOS versions, at a minimum, where essential system update functionality has not worked.  Sigh.
$ diskutil apfs convert disk27
Converting the volume on disk27 to an APFS Volume on an APFS Container
Started APFS operation on disk27 (Smash)
Converting HFS Volume to an APFS Container which will export one APFS Volume
The target is the Journaled HFS+ volume "Smash" on disk27 backed via CoreStorage on disk10s2
Checking booter partition disk10s3
The target is a data disk; it is not a macOS system disk
No APFS EFI driver found to install
Saving encryption context
The target is encrypted
Unmounting disk27
Starting conversion from HFS to APFS
Performing apfs_hfs_convert -x --verbose=0x400 /dev/disk10s2
Reporting post-conversion statistics
A problem occurred during conversion from HFS to APFS
APFS Converter exit code is 1
Aborted conversion in commit mode so will restore type

Not mounting APFS Volume
Exiting conversion operations with error code -69860

Underlying error: 1

+-> Logical Volume BC304645-7D99-481E-931F-855B3011D89D
---------------------------------------------------
Disk: disk27
Status: Online
Size (Total): 1999702634496 B (2.0 TB)
Revertible: No
LV Name: Smash
Volume Name: Smash
Content Hint: Apple_HFS
But what’s even worse about this dumpster fire is that macOS 27 can mount these volumes just fine – it’s just that all the normal ways to do it are completely broken.  If you go down to a lower level and run mount_hfs directly, it does work:
$ sudo mkdir -p /Volumes/Smash
$ sudo mount_hfs -o rdonly /dev/disk27 /Volumes/Smash
$ ls /Volumes/Smash
Documents Pictures Scratch space
That said… that -o rdonly parameter… in principle it shouldn’t be required, but I could not get macOS 27 to let me mount any HFS-on-CoreStorage volume as read-write – no matter what I did, it always fails with error “Resource busy” (EBUSY). I spent a lot of time trying to debug this, and could find no evidence of anything having the volume in question open (nothing in lsof etc).
But wait, it gets worse.
macOS 27 can’t even erase the volume.  All the normal tools – diskutil, Disk Utility, etc – fail with that same “Resource busy” error.
Workaround
Thankfully, with the help of Gemini 4 Argon, I did find a workaround. It’s convoluted, but takes only a few steps, thankfully.
First, while if you try to delete the logical volume group it ostensibly fails, it doesn’t completely fail – it does actually delete the logical volume(s) within:
$ diskutil cs delete 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
Started CoreStorage operation
Unmounting Logical Volumes
Destroying Logical Volume Group
Erasing disk10s2
newfs_hfs: cannot create filesystem on /dev/rdisk10s2: Resource busy
Mounting disk
Could not mount disk10s2 after erase
Error: -69832: File system formatter failed
1 💣 $ diskutil cs list
CoreStorage logical volume groups (1 found)
|
+-- Logical Volume Group 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
=========================================================
Name: Smash
Status: Offline
Size: 2000054960128 B (2.0 TB)
Free Space: -none-
|
+-< Physical Volume 1B5A1754-184B-4F17-A797-BF69B4BB627F
----------------------------------------------------
(No properties)
$ diskutil cs delete 0DC0EFB1-23CC-45BC-B37D-C1BBEBDAFCEB
Started CoreStorage operation
Destroying Logical Volume Group
Error: -69783: Unable to delete the CoreStorage Logical Volume Group
You still can’t destroy it completely, nor can you erase the physical volume yet – the “Resource busy” errors persist. But, the trick is to restart – after that, you can then erase the volume.
So it seems that whatever broken thing is holding the physical volume (or logical volume group) in a ‘busy’ state is tied to the existence of the logical volume(s) therein, and once they’re deleted (and the machine rebooted) the bug stops being triggered.
Call for better workarounds
I’ve glossed over a lot of debugging and attempts I made to save the volume in-place, by either making it work as-is (even if only with e.g. hfsutils) or by converting it to APFS, but neither I nor Gemini 4 Argon could find anything that worked. It’s too late for me – I was forced to just delete all my HFS+ & CoreStorage volumes and rebuild them painstakingly from backups – but if anyone finds a way, I’d love to amend this post, for the benefit of future readers.
- The problem remains the same in macOS 27 – so three major macOS versions, at a minimum, where essential system update functionality has not worked.  Sigh.
$ diskutil apfs convert disk27
Converting the volume on disk27 to an APFS Volume on an APFS Container
Started APFS operation on disk27 (Smash)
Converting HFS Volume to an APFS Container which will export one APFS Volume

Reddit tests ads in search results as traffic declines and growth concerns mount
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
19:24:37 UTC
04:24:37 KST

Just days after warning investors about declining search traffic and a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast, Reddit is looking for more ways to make money from its existing users. On Tuesday, the company announced that it’s beginning to test ad placements in its search results pages, allowing advertisers to reach users as they search for products, recommendations, and other information on its platform.
“Ads in search may appear based on a range of factors, including contextual relevance to a user’s search query,” Reddit shared in its announcement about the new ad placements. “This is an initial test with a select group of eligible advertisers. During this test, we will evaluate and understand how users respond to these ads so we can refine the experience for users and advertisers over time.”
The company offered examples of what sort of ads might appear, suggesting that a search for “espresso station” might display ads for espresso machines, coffee, or mugs, while a search for “home office setup” could surface ads for things like monitors, desks, and office chairs.
The ad test comes at a time when Reddit is reckoning with how AI has been changing the web’s landscape, and subsequently its reach.
Despite beating Wall Street’s estimates for revenue and earnings per share, the company’s stock dropped after it reported its third-quarter results last week, with fourth-quarter guidance that predicted sales of $1 billion to $1.03 billion, below expectations of $1.05 billion. This was tied to Reddit’s declining search traffic referrals resulting from Google’s move to an AI-powered search experience. AI search now sends less traffic to publishers’ websites, as features like AI Mode provide answers directly on Google’s Search Result pages, reducing clicks to other websites.
Reddit also said that its global daily active users were flat quarter-over-quarter in Q3, reaching 130.3 million, while U.S. daily active users dropped from 53.2 million in Q2 to 50.7 million in the quarter, and were down 2% year-over-year. The company noted that if the trend continues, daily active users could decline to a low double-digit percentage by the fourth quarter.
This leaves the company needing to earn more revenue from its existing users, which is where these new ads come in. The ads could prove to be more valuable to Reddit after it makes its planned shift to a logged-in experience, which was also announced during earnings. The company said it will make the transition gradually, initially in markets outside the U.S.
The decision to limit its content to logged-in users serves multiple purposes — it protects Reddit’s site from unauthorized AI scraping, and it increases its value to advertisers. Logged-in users are worth more to advertisers because they provide additional signals about their interests and behavior, allowing for better-targeted, more profitable ads.

Ten years later, ‘Pokémon Go to the polls’ still haunts the internet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
19:04:52 UTC
04:04:52 KST

In the lead-up to a presidential election that would irrefutably transform American culture, Hillary Clinton took the stage at a rally in Virginia as she campaigned to become the first female president.
“We’re going to have a lot of jobs — jobs from building infrastructure to coding. Creating new apps,” she said. “I don’t know who created Pokémon GO, but I’m trying to figure out how we get them to have Pokémon Go to the polls.”
Ten years later, it is once again Election Day in the United States. Now, most app developers aren’t even writing their own code anymore, thanks to AI, and Pokémon GO has been sold to a company wholly owned by Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund. The only thing about that political moment that hasn’t changed is that “Pokémon Go to the polls” memes still crop up on every Election Day.
“It was very bold and confident, and also just sounded so terribly out of touch and corny,” Cesar Ruiz de Castilla, an elected ward committee member in Philadelphia, told TechCrunch. “I don’t know if the mainstream media cared that much about it, but everyone was making a meme about it and talking about it online.”
Since then, digital culture has become increasingly inextricable from the fate of American politics. Donald Trump tweeted his way through his first term, then later started his own social media platform; presidential campaigns hire meme managers; the White House invites podcasters and content creators to press briefings; Elon Musk even spun up his own advisory group under Trump that named itself after the cutesy doge meme and then slashed international aid programs.
“The 2016 election was such a monumental moment in internet history, and we were all there for it — our politics have become more, not just divided, but segmented online,” Organizer Memes, a political influencer who teaches Gen Z activists how to reach their peers online via memes, told TechCrunch. “It’s a relic of an optimistic, bygone political era.”
Now, people who weren’t even old enough to vote in 2016 reflect on the year as a cultural turning point, even calling it “the last good year.” It’s a sentiment that isn’t so much political as it is rooted in nostalgia for an era of internet culture before AI slop, when we used social media to connect with friends, rather than doomscrolling through an algorithmic feed of people we don’t even follow.
At the start of the new year, this yearning for the old internet became a viral sentiment as millions of people shared throwback photos from 2016 on Instagram.
Spotify reported that user-generated playlists featuring 2016 in their titles spiked 790% in the first three weeks of the year, and the company changed its Instagram bio at the time to say it’s “romanticizing 2016 again.”
Never mind that, at the time, the internet perceived 2016 as a cursed year, even before the election — months earlier, one Slate columnist wondered how 2016 compared to 1348, the year the Black Death took hold in Europe.
“[Pokémon Go to the polls] is in that era of the singular internet, when Facebook and Twitter and Tumblr were all kind of bouncing content back-and-forth and not just this complete anarchic mess of 25 platforms that we now have and don’t use,” Organizer Memes said.
Organizer Memes also notes that some cultural touchstones that felt more significant then — like the obsession with Harambe the gorilla — haven’t had as much staying power as “Pokémon Go to the polls.”
Perhaps this is because we’re bound to remember “Pokémon Go to the polls” every few years on Election Day, and because it appeals to both sides of the aisle. On the right, it’s a way to make fun of Democrats, and on the left, it’s a shared groan of embarrassment.
“It’s like if all the kids in a class are making a joke, and then the teacher gets in on the joke, and it stops being funny,” Mack Finkel, who canvassed at the polls on Tuesday on behalf of a healthcare workers’ union, told TechCrunch. “I think there’s a key essence of millennial cringe happening here, and it’s the same reason that all my friends are rewatching [HBO’s] ‘Girls.’”
Clinton’s decade-old, corny comment can be seen as a precursor to the “Kamala is brat” meme. While the former vice president’s record as a prosecutor initially made her unpopular among some left-leaning young voters, they rallied around her once she became the only alternative to Trump. Gen Z rallied around Harris by creating flashy, absurdist “fan cam”-style edits of the candidate’s best quips in the aesthetic of Charli XCX’s album “Brat,” which soundtracked the summer of 2024.
“Previously the views I saw about Harris were making fun of her being a cop, like her history as attorney general in California with truancy laws,” Jess Rauchberg, an assistant professor of communications at the University of Leeds, told TechCrunch at the time. “Now we see that same style of memeification, but it’s an endorsement.”
It’s hard to say why “Pokémon Go to the polls” jokes still make us laugh — whether we’re mocking Clinton or expressing solidarity with others who keep showing up to vote, even as each passing year leaves us feeling more cynical.
“Pokémon Go to the polls” is a way of urging others to make the time to vote and take Election Day seriously, while still acknowledging disappointment with aging lawmakers who don’t know what it’s like to come of age in the social media era. It’s shrouded in enough irony to project a sense of jaded detachment, yet remains a desperate, earnest plea to our friends: Please, just go vote.

According to Fujifilm, "major cloud service and data center operators" have been expanding their use of magnetic tape because it can store large data volumes at relatively low cost. Tape backups can be easily disconnected and stored in a drawer, a vault, or a separate facility. Fujifilm highlights the ability to air-gap tape cartridges as a last defense for user data: "Given the sophistication of cyberattacks, magnetic tape is attracting increasing attention as a means of protecting data from threats such as ransomware."

Ferrari’s controversial Luce EV is sold out for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
18:51:33 UTC
03:51:33 KST

The Luce, Ferrari’s first electric car and one of its most polarizing models, isn’t just selling. It’s selling out.
The five-seater EV designed by Jony Ive, Apple’s longtime design chief, was mocked and widely panned when it debuted in May, sending Ferrari’s stock price lower. But all that criticism hasn’t dampened demand, according to CEO Benedetto Vigna.
The 2027 production run of the Luce, which starts at about $615,000, is “fully allocated,” Vigna said Tuesday during the company’s third-quarter earnings call, meaning every car Ferrari plans to build next year already has a buyer. “If someone comes, he has to wait one year to get the cars,” Vigna added. The first deliveries of the Luce are expected to begin in the fourth quarter.
Just how many Luce cars that represents is unclear. Ferrari has never publicly disclosed how many Luce vehicles it plans to produce. Financial Times reported earlier this year, citing unnamed sources, that Ferrari planned to sell just under 500 units this year. The company’s longer-term target is to sell 2,500 units by 2030, or about 600 a year, according to Financial Times.
Speculation on who these buyers are — ahem, the founders of multibillion-dollar AI labs, perhaps? — will have to remain just that until Luces are spotted in the wild. Vigna wouldn’t provide a breakdown of who these Luce customers are, only noting it was a “good mix in terms of client, it is a good mix also in terms of geography.” He later added that there is no specific pattern or demographic of Luce buyers.
While Luce deliveries have yet to begin, Ferrari’s existing lineup and growing demand for personalized options helped fuel its financial performance in the third quarter. Revenue from customizations, which executives said accounted for more than 21% of revenue from cars and spare parts, helped boost profits. The company said deliveries of the F80, its limited-run hypercar, and customization reflect its clients’ “ever-deepening desire” to make each Ferrari uniquely their own. As a result, the company raised its full-year guidance, saying it now expects adjusted earnings of at least €3 billion ($3.36 billion), up from €2.97 billion.
Ferrari, which enjoys some of the highest profit margins in the auto industry, reported third-quarter revenue of €1.9 billion, up 7% from a year earlier, and net income of €431 million, up 13%. Operating profit was €563 million, for an operating margin of 29.7%, meaning the company kept roughly 30 cents of every dollar of revenue as profit from its core business.

Netflix’s new AI Discover tab helps you find something to watch based on your mood

Netflix announced on Tuesday that it’s rolling out a new “AI Discover” tab where users will be able to experiment with new ways to find their next watch. The first experimental feature launching under the tab will allow users to get recommendations based on what they’re currently in the mood for.
Users can choose from curated themes featuring clips from shows and movies, based on their mood, viewing preferences, how much time they have, or what’s new and trending. Themes include “something light,” “scare me,” “family movie night,” “quick watches,” and more.
The addition of the new tab suggests that Netflix wants to make its growing library easier to navigate while shifting discovery away from an experience where users are endlessly scrolling through titles toward a more personalized and AI-powered experience.
Netflix says AI Discover is powered by a new intelligence layer it’s been building that responds to what users tell the platform in real time and keeps learning.
Once users pick a theme, they’ll see matching recommendations. They also have the option to select more specific themes so they can keep searching until they find something they’re interested in, or choose the “something different” option to start over. Each title features a “Tune Your Recommendations” button beside “Play” and “My List” to allow users to save recommendations they like or exclude titles they don’t want suggested again.
“There’s more to enjoy and discover on Netflix than ever, but what sounds right for a quiet night in may look different for family movie night or a few spare minutes,” Netflix wrote in a blog post. “We’ve spent years refining how you discover, with recommendations tailored to your tastes, from what you Thumbs Up to what you add to ‘My List.’ Now, AI Discover joins the mix as a new way to explore.”
Netflix describes AI Discover as its “test kitchen,” where it will “try out new recipes for discovery.” The company says users’ feedback will help it decide which features to keep or improve before bringing them over to the main Netflix experience.
AI Discover is starting to roll out in the U.S. to users who use Netflix in English on supported TVs. The company plans to bring the new tab to additional users in the coming weeks.
If users have access to the new feature, they’ll see a “Discover” button with a red gem icon and a “New” label in the top navigation bar on their TV.

Apple’s latest watchOS beta includes its new always-on Audio Intelligence features
Audio Intelligence lets Siri ‘rewind’ and summarize audio from your Watch’s mic.
Apple is also releasing its redesigned Health app for testing today in the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and announced expanded language support in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese. When it comes to the implications of an ambient, always-listening AI, Apple has released this Audio Intelligence

OpenAI says ChatGPT is catching up to Google in search
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
18:30:42 UTC
03:30:42 KST

In many circles, “Ask Chat” has replaced “Google it,” and that’s reflected in a new announcement from OpenAI: the volume of search queries run through ChatGPT now equals 20 percent of the volume run through Google.
OpenAI says ChatGPT is catching up to Google in search
ChatGPT processes one-fifth the volume of search queries as Google, per OpenAI.
Adam Fry, OpenAI’s consumer product lead for ChatGPT, made the announcement at a press event on Monday. He said the company defines a search as any time a user inputs a query that results in a web search, as opposed to tasks like defining a term or a simple how-to explanation. (Fry did not specify the source of the Google search volume number.)
Having one-fifth as many searches as Google is still a long way from overtaking it, but for comparison, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said during Google’s 2023 antitrust trial that Bing had about 3 percent of the search engine market share after trying for more than a decade. During the trial, Google described AI as a potential disruptor, arguing ChatGPT was poised to seriously compete with it — now, OpenAI seems to agree. (OpenAI likely uses Microsoft Bing for a significant part of its searches, along with its in-house search index, although there is still some speculation that it routes some queries through Google.)
The news comes amid an ongoing search engine shake-up, as Google continues to reduce conventional referrals to third-party sites and invests heavily in AI tools — not just AI Overview but also additional generative AI capabilities, including personalized search results with visualizations and charts. But as search queries increasingly route through OpenAI and other AI labs’ services, other companies are investing in the same types of AI-focused search experience, even if they call it something else: for OpenAI, it’s “Intelligent UI,” or creating a visual and interactive interface within a chatbot response. “That’s where the future of this technology goes. You’re talking to a canvas,” Fry said.
Much like Google, OpenAI sees a potential path to profitability through ads, particularly as it approaches an IPO potentially slated for early next year. OpenAI has defended its ads in the past, and Fry told reporters they hadn’t produced a lasting backlash. “Ads have not negatively impacted the product or the usage of the product,” he said, adding that “most people do not seem to mind ads in the product.”
OpenAI announced last month that the company would begin introducing images of sponsored products and services in ChatGPT rather than just a company’s name, logo, and a link to its product like before.
“Ads have maybe shown us that we could be doing this more, actually,” Fry said.

Indie games are missing launch dates because Steam is backed up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
18:14:50 UTC
03:14:50 KST

Many indie game developers have recently posted on social media about unexpectedly long approval wait times for their game submissions on Steam, with some of the approvals causing developers to miss their planned launch dates.
Indie games are missing launch dates because Steam is backed up
One developer has been waiting for weeks on approval for a game it planned to release today.
For example, Studio Daimon, the team behind an upcoming title called Food Devils, had planned to launch the game in early access today after submitting its build on October 12th. But the game is “still awaiting approval,” according to a post from game director Alfred Kamon. “Even now, we don’t know when Steam will give us the final OK to finally release our game. We sent another ticket last week saying that the situation was urgent and that we might miss our release date because of this, but it also got ignored.”
In October, publisher 2 Left Thumbs said it missed its planned launch of Wheel Make It “by nearly two weeks” due to the long wait for build reviews. You can read some details about the studio’s setbacks, including failing a review for a “one single option in the menu” not being accessible with a controller, in a Steam post. There are lots of other recent posts about review build waits as well.
Valve says on a Steam developer website that a review of a game’s store presence “typically takes 3-5 business days to complete,” though the company suggests submitting a page for review “at least 7 business days before you want it live to account for potential changes you’ll need to make.”
However, as of late, Steam has seemingly been grappling with a sharp increase in games; October’s Steam Next Fest had 7,240 games, a 65.2 percent increase over June’s Steam Next Fest, according to How to Market a Game. A Reddit user also found that 49.9 percent of all games released since Valve started asking developers in 2024 to label games that use AI now have an AI disclosure.
Kamon and 2 Left Thumbs suspect the longer waits are due to “slop” slowing down the process. “We can only assume it’s because Steam’s review queue is clogged up by AI slop, but the whole process is now taking several weeks for some developers,” said Kamon.
In a new post from Valve published after we first ran this story, the company acknowledged that following a “a significant increase in submissions for store and page review in recent months,” it’s “running a little behind right now” and taking “up to 12 business days” for reviews, saying that much of the delay is “having to re-review games.” It has updated its release checklist for developers, including requiring them to run a game through Steam for at least five minutes. Valve also says that further improvements are on the way for the build review process.
Itch.io has also been dealing with a rise in games, with the platform saying last weekend that “The number of game pages being created per-day has doubled in the past 2 months.” Last night, the platform said it “Just deleted a couple terabytes of ai slop 😌”
Update, November 3rd: Added new post from Valve.

Google’s Gemini-powered Home Speaker is already on sale for 20 percent off

Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
18:11:49 UTC
03:11:49 KST

If you’re looking for a good smart speaker, the Google Home Speaker is down to around $79 ($20 off) in all four colors at Best Buy, Walmart, and Target. That’s the best price we’ve seen for the Gemini-powered speaker, which launched in June and represents Google’s first smart speaker in several years.
Google’s Gemini-powered Home Speaker is already on sale for 20 percent off
Google’s latest smart speaker offers surprisingly good sound for its size, Gemini-powered voice controls, and more.
In her review, my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy noted that Google’s new Home Speaker offers a nice balance of sound quality, size, and design. It’s smaller than the prior-gen Nest Audio, making it easy to place anywhere in your home. However, despite its small size, it produces loud, clear audio with 360-degree sound. Our own David Pierce even found it sounded cleaner, louder, and sharper than Amazon’s similarly priced Echo Dot Max, though Tuohy preferred the latter’s fuller sound and stronger bass. The older Nest Audio still sounds better overall, but Google’s latest speaker takes up less space and costs slightly less.
The Google Home Speaker also offers a few useful smart home upgrades. It supports Matter and includes a Thread border router, allowing you to connect and control a wide range of compatible smart home devices. It’s also the first Google smart speaker that can double as an audio output for the Google TV Streamer 4K, letting you play TV audio through one or two speakers instead of your TV’s built-in speakers. Tuohy found it worked well and delivered clear dialogue, though sound quality varied depending on what she was watching.
One of its most notable features is support for Gemini, which is also available on older Google speakers and is much better at understanding natural language and complex requests than the old Google Assistant. In her testing, Tuohy found it could handle multiple smart home commands at once and respond to conversational requests, like turning down the air conditioner when she mentioned feeling too hot. It’s also particularly impressive at answering general knowledge questions, though it can be slow and unreliable at times. Keep in mind, too, that some features require a $10-a-month Google Home Premium subscription, including Gemini Live, which lets you have extended conversations with the assistant without repeating the wake word.

I use AI (Oct 2026)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
18:11:11 UTC
03:11:11 KST

How I use AI (Oct 2026)
Wow, things have changed.
Last October, I took stock of how I was using AI — specifically the cool stuff like LLMs that we call 'AI’. I’m so glad I did. Things are very, very different 12 months later.
Background
I still believe I use AI fairly typically, but I’ve had a notable change in background. Last October, I was an engineer on Microsoft’s Windows AI team. I am now a research engineer at Salesforce AI Research. I spend more time supporting scientists & building rapid prototypes, rather than working with a large team of engineers. I spend about ~$3,000/month in tokens.
In any case, I mostly use AI in the same ways as last year:
- Coding
- Research & search
- Summarization & transcription & (new) voice
- Writing
- Art & music & (new) video
Also new this year, I’ve drafted a personal AI policy; we’ll start there.
As before, this remains purely my opinion & speculation. If you use AI differently, let me know!
My AI policy
This year I began drafting a personal AI policy — as in, a document for how I want to use AI in my life. I am very excited about it. I am also working on an explicit AI policy for this site (still thinkin’; probably based on Hank Green’s policy), but a personal policy is to give me a framework for using these tools day-to-day.
AI leaks into life. Teammates ask Claude to write their Slack messages, grandparents generate creepy memes of their grandchildren, and researchers delegate their thinking to machines. I’ve seen all of these things; even strong creators like Hank Green and BrainPOP get lost.
Humans clearly do not have norms for using these tools, and we’re messing up. I hope that a personal policy will ground me as AI becomes smarter. I hope to adapt that policy over time, and I’m eager to see how it evolves. I’m also open to draft 1 being utterly, hopelessly wrong.
Ultimately, I want to spend my life making cool things with other people. AI can help, AI can hurt. A policy helps me find the difference.
Coding
Writing code is solved.
Last year, I waxed poetic about how GitHub Copilot autocomplete transformed how I write code.
Well, uh, I no longer write much code. Agentic coding has made it obsolete.
My workday now means managing ~5–6 Claude Code (or OpenCode or Codex or Pi) agents. I’ll give Claude a feature to implement, or a bug to reproduce, or any other task I used to do by hand; each agent gets its own copy of the code (a Git worktree, if you’re technical), then just… gets to work. The agents write code, run tests, even create & review PRs.
They are nothing short of magic:
- They let me build fast: agents will prototype any new feature in ~20 minutes. I truly cannot count the number of features, bugfixes, tests, and tools I’ve (AI’ve?) been able to build because of these agents. For example, AI let me test confusing audio code on macOS and iOS in just a few minutes.
- They let me try crazy things: human teams aim to “fail fast”; agents can fail ultra-fast. I’m happy to test crazy new ideas and throw out what doesn’t work well. It was able to wire & test a huge change to Mumble that added better noise cancelling; I use my beta build of it nearly every day.
- They remove drudgery: I’ve had agents diagnose & fix urgent bugs with nothing more than a description and a “please fix!” while I continued working on other things.
- They let me be kinder: since agents write everything, it is simple to propose sweeping changes to my teammates during code review, or even write my own versions — both things unthinkable in the era of hand-written code.
I do not believe engineering is solved: left to run on their own, agents will build poorly-functioning, over-architected, unreadable, self-congratulatory piles of slop. Every friend I’ve asked agrees that agents still need human taste and experience to produce good work. Some of that is minutiae (like that annoying status dot Claude likes to throw onto sites), but most of it is critical. Agents tend to get lost on their own. My most successful work this year was hand-writing a tool, replacing ~4,000 lines of vibe-code with a few hundred. My system has proven more flexible, easier to test, and more generalizable than what it replaced.
It remains to be seen how long that human edge will last, though.
I also now reckon with the fatigue of using these agents. Managing 6 different conversations with 6 different robots about 6 different features is overstimulating & exhausting in a way that coding never was. When I started using agents, I remember rushing to answer their questions like they were human colleagues waiting for help! While I have tempered that anthropomorphic bias, it’s exhausting to juggle so many problems at once. The allure of sending just one more prompt before lunch… then dinner… oy. There is also, as I wrote in Consider the chairmaker, the decline of craft. My friend Peter laments ceding the joy of programming to machines: for many of us, honing the code, finding the right design, seeing the parts mesh together — that was the meditative purpose we found in our jobs. Now, we rarely write anything. We instead delegate it to agent number 7.
But let me return to the joy of working with agents: they are so fast, so open to feedback, and so intelligent. Working with them can be utterly delightful.
For example, while I was building a harness for voice agents, one programming agent decided (correctly) that my simple test harness was insufficient. So it used my Mac’s built-in text-to-speech to directly test the voice agent it was building. Then, newer agents started doing it, too. Either they had documented the technique, or they were each smart enough to independently discover it. Directly testing the product they were building. Absolutely brilliant.
Agents frequently recommend knobs & settings that I’ll reject for being too complex and unnecessary — and, voilà, I’ll need the knob next week. Silly human!
Anyway, because of agentic coding, agentic pull requests are increasingly the way I review agent code. “Make a draft PR,” I write, “I’ll review it soon!” And review it I do — agents still aren’t reliable enough to trust without validating, so I’ll still review their code & test it manually. However, I don’t do the “line-by-line” code reviews I used to do with humans. I focus instead on architecture, on larger patterns in the code. Are there systemic issues with an approach? Should I add new agent guidance to CLAUDE.md? Can I build better test harnesses, so the machines can test their own code?
Agentic code review is surprisingly helpful here: I try to write rules for the code review robots whenever I notice a recurring issue with generated code, so the agents will identify & fix issues by themselves. One rule I enjoyed creating: a "Claude-y comment detector." You think my writing is verbose? Try Claude’s.
On more typical engineering teams, human code review seems increasingly difficult. A friend of mine complained that his teammates simply ask “their” Claudes to review code written by other Claudes. An ouroboros of Claudes! Agents catch bugs & stylistic issues very well, but they are abysmal at designing architecture. Agentic code review is certainly not a replacement for humans yet.
Last year, I was skeptical of inline editing and code mode, both features of GitHub Copilot. They were not very useful then, and they are even less useful with agents. I have removed them from the table.
Research & search
Last year, I was excited about research & search: they were the most frequent reason I used ChatGPT. Now, generative AI is the default way I do those things.
The biggest change has been Google’s AI summary. Google’s first or second result is almost always an AI summary, and it’s usually decent. So my traditional search is now AI-first by default. Is it perfect? Absolutely not. In one day, it gave me incorrect URLs for NPR’s RSS feeds and couldn’t find the origin of “AI’ve”.
But none of the top results clearly gave me NPR’s RSS feeds either, and even Claude couldn’t find “AI’ve”. Meanwhile, searching “HP Reverb G2” gave me the specs I was looking for, “ai intelligence is spiky” pointed me to the correct term (“jagged”), “emoji sigh” gave me the right emoji without sending me to a scummy site, and “rel nofollow markdown” reminded me how to link that site without giving them search engine juice.
Product search is still mediocre. I’ll look at the summary when I search “best hysa”, but I don’t trust Gemini to have good advice on where to put my money. Claude certainly helped me explore budget VR options and understand technical details about grease for KitchenAid mixers, but can I trust its coffee table recommendations? Sleeper sofas? Let’s not even mention how uncomfortable it is to see ads in my ChatGPT chats.
Pub facts—stuff I’d ask my wife at a pub — remain awesome with LLMs. Again, Google’s AI summary means “lego cat on a balcony tiktok guy” will help me find @avadonye’s precarious LEGO builds, and “art vtuber who is a lizard on TikTok who gives short tutorials” will help me find Mallow, the art vtuber who is a lizard on TikTok who gives short tutorials.
I often avoid using LLMs for pub facts, in the same way I generally avoided Google for them before, because I like puzzling with my friends. I like Fermi problems.
But I’m more and more excited about using LLMs as teachers to explore well-known concepts. I breezed over this last year, but that is unfair to LLMs. I believe they are the greatest teachers humanity has ever created.
- I had an LLM walk me step-by-step through fine-tuning Mistral to speak like a pirate (yarrr).
- I used Claude to practice responding to an EMS call I heard on the radio.
- I had Claude use a socractic method skill I found via Dan MacKinlay to help me brainstorm new approaches for semantic endpointing (knowing when a user is done speaking) in voice agents.
- I asked Claude to explain typical approaches to a complex legal document.
- I’ve even had Claude quiz me on a long code review, to ensure I understood what the agent had written. The open-source project Mumble actually added a similar quiz to their AGENTS.md a few weeks ago.
I am actually jealous of the endless care & patience that these machines show. I hope we discover how to share this patience with our kids while ensuring our kids still learn. Veritasium’s Derek Muller discusses this in What Everyone Gets Wrong About AI and Learning: AI is incredible at drilling repetitive practice, at giving immediate feedback, of all the things a private tutor can do… if you ask it to.
“The world is full of heavy objects,” he says, “and yet most people are not ripped.”
That is my greatest fear with AI tutoring today. That these machines must be reminded to teach. Per Muller, learning requires Type 2 thinking — enaging the slow, reasoning mode of your brain. This is very difficult. Your body will surreptitiously & continuously nudge you out of this mode. Tutors exist to force you back into it. But ChatGPT exists to do things for you: it is so fine-tuned for that use that it tends to forget “it’s meant to be a tutor”, even when previously asked. What learning may occur when you have both forgotten your desire to learn?
This differs from my biggest concern last year: accuracy. Responses then often had basic factual errors, but that seems less of an issue today. I think there are 2 basic factors:
- I am more AI-literate. I think more of us have a “sense” of what AI can do well, so we avoid the jagged edges. I don’t, for example, trust ChatGPT’s ability to read sparsely-digitized documents from 1867. So I asked hopefully, then basically ignored its findings.
- AI is smarter. Just like in coding, I think we hit an inflection point this year, where models are simply smart enough to answer more things reliably. MAJOR spoilers for Control if you click, but there’s a reason Google’s AI summary of its ending (using Gemini 3, from November 2025) is simple and correct while Bing’s (using ~GPT 4o, from May 2024) is not, conflating the game with its sequel.
This trend extends to literature searches. Last year, I shared my trepidation about using LLMs for complex literature searches. My skepticism remains: these machines have access to everything ever written, so they can support any premise in good faith. Also, it is well-demonstrated that LLMs have default bias, politically or in other fields, like business strategy. I am worried about their ability to subtly impose worldview, either on their own or at the behest of corporations and governments.
Yet LLMs are now my first choice for literature searches. That’s partially because Google searches have that AI summary on top, so I end up reading it, but also because LLMs have been much more effective than traditional search at finding good, nuanced data for me — despite potential bias. You must remember that Google Scholar search kinda sucks: when I started researching Car touchscreens are cheap, not good, for months I could not find any studies beyond one done by an auto magazine—Vi Bilägare. That was despite having worked at a Georgia Tech lab that researched car user interfaces! Especially as they’ve gotten smarter & I’ve developed intuition, LLMs are good finders. Just see Claude’s investigation into human perceptions of latency for me:
Ultimately, though, human experts are still more reliable than agents. That’s how I moved forward with “Car touchscreens”—I asked someone from that GT lab. I’ve also been buying more books, even slightly-obsolete ones like Card, Morgan, & Newell’s The Psychology of Human-Computer Interaction (everyone, including LLMs, cite it) or old editions of Wicken’s Engineering Psychology and Human Performance (via a nuclear consultant I met at a wedding). They ground my research, simply by offering a legible worldview.
And that’s why I’ve been disappointed in AI as collaborator for novel research. AI has harmed some research I’ve been doing.
My team at Salesforce has been working on voice stuff, and I’ve been trying to improve turn detection — understanding when a user is done speaking. That’s a hard problem, and it’s been a great opportunity to read fundamental research on how human conversation works (finally!). AI was great at finding that research and good datasets (though my teammates gave me context the AI never did). And it was great when I asked it to use the Socratic method to help me design my own turn detection model — until, on a whim, I asked: “are there better architectures?” Why yes, yes there were. AI had led me astray.
That’s not the only time AI waylaid me. LLMs could not figure out how to annotate that model’s training data correctly. I spent days going back and forth with them, trying to decide how to separate turns from interruptions. It is embarrassing how simple the problem became after one good discussion with a human teammate. LLMs are not yet good companions when brainstorming complicated things.
It is weird to write this when OpenAI just solved a Millenium Problem, proved a weaker version of another, solved hundreds more, and releases more solutions every day. But those results cost “millions of dollars”: you need to burn tokens, having agents review agents review agents… just to produce something coherent. In my case, I find I enter this “AI fog” where it takes more effort to review the agent’s response than to come up with my own answers.
It is obvious that AI researchers are coming. Just… not today, not with me.
Summarization & transcription & voice
LLMs (and local models!) remain uninterestingly good at summarization & transcription.
I’ve been using OpenWhispr and Handy to dictate to my computer, especially to talk to my agents. The best models on the planet run on your computer locally, for free. My biggest complaint is that the apps have bugs (hotkeys work inconsistently, etc.). It’s hard to describe a more boring type of success.
My meetings have automatic notes. My friend built a local pipeline to transcribe & search his childhood home videos. Vikram Oberoi built a site (in 2024!) that automatically transcribes NYC city hall meetings. You can do all of these things on your Mac.
However, I have yet to reliably use voice beyond dictation.
There’s a reason my team at Salesforce is researching it: voice is the original modality. It should be a seamless way of talking to these human-like robots. But I have never felt compelled to talk to my robots; it’s never been frictionless or private-feeling or useful enough. Does old-school Siri count?
Writing
Last year: “ew.” This year: “ew.”
I still do not use AI to write from scratch, nor as an outlining aid, for things I make.
I’ve narrowed this rule a bit from last year. Last year, I argued that LLMs always lacked context and so were poor communicators. With agentic coding, that’s changed. So I’ve had agents document experiments I designed but had no hand in executing, or write READMEs for code they generated end-to-end.
But even that limited exception irks me. I do not like when I stumble upon AI-generated spew, so why should I subject others to it? To that end, I’ve started prompting my agents to identify themselves whenever they write prose, and I often end up rewriting their documents myself (or at least adding an executive summary). That has helped, but I’m not certain it is enough.
In general, I’m surprised how bad AI remains at writing. AI writing is demanding to read: usually plodding, repetitive, and vapid — but then randomly terse and vague, like it doesn’t understand its own words. Agents will so often cite & quote & summarize every paper ever published, then synthesize it all into a mound of nonsense. That is the AI fog I hit: do I misunderstand all these new papers, or did the LLM just serve up some pseudo-profound bullshit? It is bewildering to me that these models can solve generational math problems on one hand, yet utterly fail to describe turn-taking behavior in humans on the other. That is, I guess, their jagged intelligence. They do not reason like we do. They cannot be fine-tuned to speak like we do. So they solve problems we cannot, and share them in reports we struggle to understand.
In any case, it should not be surprising that I do not use AI for writing or outlining in my communication; neither at work nor on this blog. My employer pays me for my ideas, which only I can voice. And I write on this blog for fun. Writing is an art and a skill I enjoy pursuing.
Why would I delegate my voice to a machine that writes tedious dreck?
It’s still great for finding words. Google AI talked me out of writing “hawking off” (which is not an expression) instead of “ceding” later on. But I’m tempering my regard for it as an editor. Despite my positive & worried assessment last year, when I spoke to several friends who asked agents to edit their job applications, their feedback was universally tepid. Agents were sycophantic, reluctant to be critical. And anyone who worked around this (by saying, for example, "my friend wrote this") found that agents offered misplaced, trite advice that lacked nuance. The agents seemed to regress to the mean: helping those with the worst writing and hindering those with the best. The agents were… fine.
As one friend put it:
[AI writing] is as good as it was 3 years ago. Which, when you consider how much everything else has changed since then…
I avoided using AI editors altogether this year, out of fear that they would erase my voice. But I’m increasingly certain they would just blandify it. AI tells remain the same as always (“You’re absolutely right!”), and these machines seem incapable of improvement without substantial guidance. Perhaps it’s survivorship bias, but these very smart machines produce very mediocre writing.
Art & music & video
Finally, art. I still don’t have a good use for image generation.
Last year, I used AI to generate a few odds and ends, but I stopped this year, mostly out of a vague sense of discomfort. I felt like I was ceding opportunities for creativity to the mediocrity machine.
I’ve enjoyed a lot of the low-effort memes I’ve seen; We need more data centers is one of my favorite jokes all year. And AI helped design some useful presentations I attended. But I’m not sure how AI art fits into life on Earth. Last year I thought I saw AI art at a gift shop. Well, now I’ve seen AI Sketchers ads, AI event posters, AI restaurant menus, AI logos for stores and e-sports teams, AI canvases at HomeSense, and AI t-shirts at Walmart. It’s everywhere, and it’s explicitly replacing human art. Gross.
AI music generation is perplexing in the opposite way. Last year, I worried that I would grow equally tired of it. But no! I’m really enjoying some AI music — and so is the rest of the world. The viral San Juan song inspired covers from humans and lip sync videos from “Mila Kunis, Charlie Puth and Jennifer Love Hewitt”. AI has also inspired new genres: I’ve been humming AI is normal technology? (95k views), LGTM (Looks Good to Me) (1.6M), and The Simulation’s Ending (169k) for weeks. As one commenter wrote on OMG! We’ve found other agents (120k):
I think AI art & music are beautiful when they are used as lenses for human creativity, rather than replacements for it. I guessed something similar last year, and I think last year’s music proved me right. As soon as commercialism replaced creativity, I was out. I soured on Eiden XII when they started sharing new “but it hits different” covers weekly, and I got bored of steel coils-style edutainment after hearing the first clone. There’s something cynical and manipulative about a synthetic woman belting “talk me out of dying” when some dude (presumably) makes money every time I play it.
Similarly, I haven’t listened to any of the new Doompop that’s hit my feed. It’s cool when you generate a few songs; less cool when you post every day. It feels like vultures picking ad revenue from the corpse of a good idea.
That is evident in the world of video generation. I largely escaped last year (although my mom got some weird whale-cleaning videos), but now I’m seeing a bunch. I see AI ads all the time — most memorably with horrid horse-people in Sixt ads. I got baited into a video of a fake Edna Mode lookalike & some slop WW2 history videos, and my wife got tricked by AI summaries of Adventure Time marketed as sleep aids. All of them hoping to get views, to get ad revenue, to get — as Corridor Digital puts it—“a little bit skimmed off of that YouTube trough.” It is sobering to open an AI history video in Incognito and gaze at the misleading slop recommended next to it:
It is horrid to see these machines that can mass-produce art being used to mass-produce art. And I know that seems silly, but there’s a world where we use these tools to elevate artists, just like coding agents elevate me.
I am lucky I do not make my living from art. Art remains valuable to me. Even if AI can write a song faster than I can, I still doodle, I still play piano.
Drawin' it yourself is more fun, anyway.
Conclusion
So here we are, 12 months later.
12 months since my first abortive attempts to have agents write code. 10 months since Claude Code first made me say, “wow,” when it built me an insurance comparison tool in one shot. And now machines write 90%+ of my code.
It is easy to forget how new this is. 15 months ago, AI did well at a prestigious high school math competition. 2 months ago, AI solved Navier-Stokes.
Last year, I wrote: “I’m confident we’re just starting to see what AI can achieve.” That remains true. We are just now beginning to see what these mechanized coders and mathematicians can build. My friends have built each other tools to communicate. I was able to finally clean up and share a tool I’d started in 2020. Agents helped me finish up an open-source change I’d wanted to make for years, start making an app, test massive changes to old software, and quickly understand new operating systems.
That is just the start.
It is a brave new world. Where these machines also ship corporate slop and leave mathematicians in shock. But I think of how my uncle uses these tools to build his own software; how my friends make software that helps us stay in touch; how these things have helped me learn so, so much. Tools can be used to help people.
That is how I hope to use AI.
Thanks to Peter Kreiseder and Atherai Maran for consulting. Claude helped make the status icon look more Claude-y.

Appendix: my subscriptions
In case you’re wondering, I’m subscribed to:
- Claude Pro ($17/mo)
- GitHub Copilot Pro ($10/mo)
I cancelled OpenAI about a month ago, which is crazy. OpenAI was my first AI subscription! But most of my personal usage is Claude Code, and I ended up using Claude for random questions instead of ChatGPT. And last year we thought OpenAI was so far ahead!
I use GitHub Copilot Pro solely for autocomplete.
