Anthropic IPO filing: $1.7B quarterly payroll, about $107K per employee monthly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
11:16:07 UTC
20:16:07 KST

Winners & losers: It's no secret that if you want some of the most lucrative compensation packages in tech, AI is the industry to be in. That's been perfectly illustrated by Anthropic's amended S-1 filing, which reveals its personnel costs recently averaged over $100,000 per employee per month.
The filing, spotted by Business Insider, shows that Anthropic recorded more than $1.7 billion in personnel expenses from July through to September. With 5,300 people working at the company, that works out at over $322,000 per person over the three-month span, or about $107,300 per employee per month.
Those costs include standard cash salaries along with bonuses, benefits, and employer payroll taxes. The largest share, $1.1 billion, came from Anthropic's stock-based compensation expenses, which reflect the value of company shares employees earn as part of their pay. Anthropic records that value as an expense even though employees don't receive the equivalent amount in cash.
As eye-watering as those figures sound, the wage bill takes up a much smaller slice of Anthropic's revenue than it once did. In 2023, the Claude maker spent more than twice as much on personnel as it brought in from customers. In the first nine months of 2026, personnel costs reached $4.8 billion, or about 15% of the $33.2 billion in revenue Anthropic reported for the same period.
Going public could change things pretty quickly. Anthropic has filed for what could be the biggest IPO ever. Some of its restricted stock units come with two conditions: employees have to work at the company for a certain length of time, and an event such as an IPO has to take place.
Had Anthropic completed its IPO on September 30, 2026, it says it would have recorded an $8.2 billion stock-based compensation charge that day for restricted stock units. That single charge would have exceeded the $4.86 billion Anthropic reported in personnel expenses for the first nine months of 2026. The company expected to recognize another $24.1 billion in expense for those awards over a weighted-average period of about two years, according to its amended filing.
Anthropic has some well-funded competition in the AI business. Last year, OpenAI boss Sam Altman claimed Meta had offered some of his employees $100 million signing bonuses to jump ship. Anthropic has managed to grow its workforce fivefold since the end of 2024, though that still leaves it with fewer than a tenth as many employees as Meta, which has around 67,000 people on its payroll.

Redmagic upgrades its liquid-cooled gaming phone with extra RGBs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
11:07:11 UTC
20:07:11 KST

After introducing true liquid cooling to its gaming phones last year, Redmagic is upping the ante in its 12 Pro by building RGB lights into the transparent cooling loop, too.
Redmagic upgrades its liquid-cooled gaming phone with extra RGBs
The Redmagic 12 Pro adds lights to its liquid.
The Redmagic 12 Pro adds lights to its liquid.
And they work! Sort of. The lights do turn on, and they can be set to glow in set patterns, activate for specific apps, or trigger for notifications and calls. The problem is that like last year’s 11 Pro, the cooling system itself uses fluorescent blue liquid, which the lights have to work against. Blue or white lighting just makes it look more blue, green turns out turquoise, and red or orange lights mostly produce colored bubbles swimming in a blue tide.
The liquid-cooling RGBs are joined by a few other lights across the phone, with a small ring below the main camera, a side light that shines out from inside the chassis, and thin strips on the touch-sensitive shoulder buttons. Those don’t have the liquid to work against, so they shine in the intended color and often look quite different from the cooling ring. To complete the inconsistency, there are two strips of visible liquid cooling without RGB lights in the phone’s top-right corner, around and below the Redmagic logo, so those will be blue no matter what. Good luck getting all of this to match.
The liquid cooling itself is improved beyond the lights, with output pressure of 130kPa, 85 percent up on the previous generation. It’s once again joined by both a built-in fan and a vapor chamber, which between them should be enough to keep the Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 in check.
It’s joined by 12GB or 16GB of RAM (the 24GB variant is seemingly a victim of RAMageddon) and 256GB, 512GB, or 1TB of storage. The 8,400mAh battery should last a day or two, even while powering those lights and cooling, and the 80W charging is fairly fast. There’s an IP69 rating for water and dust resistance across most of the phone, though that may not count for much since the section around the fan is only IPX8, with no rated dust protection, making for a pretty large weak point. Existing Redmagic users may also be disappointed that the 3.5mm headphone jack has disappeared.
The cameras are predictably basic, too: a pair of 50-megapixel rear cameras, one main and one ultrawide, neither with especially large sensors. The best thing about them is their design: completely flush with the phone’s body, sitting underneath the same glass panel that stretches across the rest of the rear.
The other standout spec is the 185Hz refresh rate display, though like most high refresh rate displays, it hits the max speed only during certain compatible games. Redmagic boasts that this is the first 185Hz display to feature an under-display selfie camera too, one of those achievements that’s a record by virtue of its sheer specificity. The 16-megapixel camera here is very difficult to see — it’s much less visible than the iPhone Duo’s under-display camera — but photo quality is limited. It’s good enough for video calls, but selfies look rubbish, and it uses aggressive AI beautification features that as best as I can tell are impossible to turn off, perhaps to help mask how poor the quality is otherwise.
Redmagic isn’t immune to industrywide pricing pressure, so the 12 Pro starts at $949 — a $200 increase on the 11 Pro, and $100 up on May’s 11S Pro — climbing to $1,199 for the top spec. Every version includes both liquid cooling and RGB lights at least, which wasn’t true the last time around. Preorders start November 12th, with shipping from the 18th.
Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

Cops Bust Botnet of 1.3 Million Android TV Boxes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

Cops Bust Botnet of 1.3 Million Android TV Boxes (theregister.com) 44
			
		 	
				A coalition of security firms working with Japan's National Police Agency has disrupted a botnet of more than 1.3 million Android devices across 200+ countries. "We assess with high confidence that the backdoor and botnet were intentionally developed, deployed, and operated for financial gain by Videostrong Technology," the Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a blog post. The Register reports:  Videostrong Technology is a hardware manufacturer based in Shenzhen, China. It builds Android devices, including home TV boxes and projectors. According to Google, Videostrong deliberately embedded the XCPE backdoor in device firmware and sold access to criminal affiliates, allowing them to install additional malware modules on devices shipped to unsuspecting customers. When buyers connected these devices to their home networks, the preinstalled backdoor allowed operators to create proxy networks and hide malicious traffic using the customers' internet connections without their knowledge.
The firmware's pre-installed management agent purported to be a standard remote-management client, according to TrendAI. It pulled updates from a GitHub page, and connected to a Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) server that gave the operator full remote control of each box, allowing them to install and remove apps, change settings, and push updates to the infected devices. Between June 3 and October 1, TrendAI documented more than 3.8 million distinct home and mobile IP addresses connected to the operation.
The coalition also disrupted the command-and-control domains used to manage the affiliate modules. "Because these affiliates each have diversified distribution channels for their modules beyond XCPE, we assess that taking down their C2 domains will sever access to at least 10 million additional compromised devices," according to GTIG.  Google said it had since cut ties with Videostrong, and banned the OEM from making devices with preloaded Google apps.

Bambu&#8217;s nine-nozzle H3C foretells the future of 3D printing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
09:10:07 UTC
18:10:07 KST

Three years ago, I told you how home 3D printers had evolved for speed, producing parts in minutes that used to take hours or days. Now, the next evolution is here: printers that can swap between materials on the fly, mix different colors to produce nearly the full rainbow, mix soft and hard materials, and even mix different sizes of nozzle and different diameters of filament so you can switch between high speed and fine detail in a single print.
Bambu’s nine-nozzle H3C foretells the future of 3D printing
The Bambu H3C is a tool-changing, color-mixing, nine-nozzle printer that keeps your filament dry too.
Today, Bambu Lab is announcing its most advanced 3D printer yet, the $2,499 H3C, which can do all of that mixing goodness — by loading nine different rolls of filament into nine different print heads.
Even if you’d never buy a printer this pricey, even if you’ve sworn off Bambu printers for good, the H3C is the perfect vehicle for me to explain where the state of the art in home printing tech is headed.
While the H3C still only prints in one material at any given moment, Bambu’s new “Swaptek” system lets the printer swap in any of the eight other nozzles in six seconds flat. All nine tools are stored in a rack at the front of the printer, where they can independently preheat to the correct temperature right before they’re needed.
With Bambu’s new “PLA Palette” cyan, magenta, yellow, and white filament, I printed a beautiful rainbow bird feather that emulated most of the other colors between those inks. With a mix of flexible TPU and rigid PLA filaments, I was able to print a hard wristwatch housing with an integrated flexible watchband. With an ultra-soft “75A” TPU filament plus a harder 90A variety, I printed a breathable, wearable shoe that… didn’t quite fit, unfortunately. (I’ll measure and try again.)
To be clear, Bambu didn’t invent toolchanger printers or color mixing. You could even argue Bambu’s slightly behind the curve, particularly after the $700-$900 Snapmaker U1 and its four-color, five-second swaps pleasantly surprised the community earlier this year. (Prusa also sells its hotly anticipated 8-tool INDX system for $2,249, though I’ve heard it has some issues.)
But I would have never bought previous toolchangers for myself, because they don’t have a place to keep your filament dry when you’re not printing. (Wet filament is one of the biggest remaining causes of print failures.) The H3C theoretically changes that by storing its nine rolls in an ostensibly airtight auto-loading container called the AMS 3H. Two of those nine slots even have built-in dryers that can hit 85 degrees Celsius and keep on drying your filament while you print, a big step up from Bambu’s previous AMS systems.
I haven’t tried the H3C for long enough to tell you if it’s ready to buy, and I’ve definitely run into some quirks in my first couple weeks of testing. I’ve had to start every single print twice because the printer complains that its “toolhead camera” isn’t initializing properly, I once lost half a day of printing to a false-positive print failure detection, and the beta build of Bambu Studio provided to reviewers initially got confused when I tried to mix colors. (I’m told that last one will be fixed by launch, and Bambu eventually provided some troubleshooting steps for the toolhead camera close to embargo time.)
You also have to load flexible TPU filaments into the H3C manually, and I learned the hard way that not all of the printer’s nine slots can actually accept a roll of TPU without causing trouble. Slot #6 can load standard filaments, but if you load the flexible stuff, another printhead can snag it and cause a nasty jam:
This also isn’t a printer where you can quickly repair a nozzle without tools, or use previous-gen toolless H, P, and A series swappable nozzles. It’s an all-new system that involves some minor disassembly, and I’m not sure about Bambu’s decision to leave filament in the toolheads between prints where it might attract moisture.
But so far, this seems like an easier, more reliable printer than the two-nozzle Bambu H2D was at launch. Other than the Slot #6 TPU jam, which Bambu actually warns reviewers about in a section of the reviewer’s guide that I missed reading, everything I’ve tried to print has come out great so far — and without creating a mountain of little “printer poop” waste when I switch between colors! Dramatically reduced waste is one of the benefits of having extra nozzles.
With any luck, the future of 3D printing won’t just be for hobbyists willing to figure out which colors of filament they need to order before each and every project, or obsessives who store dozens of colors in vacuum-sealed bags. Instead, it should be more like today’s inkjet printers — an entire rainbow of color, ready to go at a moment’s notice. And hopefully without all the inkjet printer shenanigans, of course.
If you like Bambu’s toolchanger system, you probably won’t have to pay $2,499 for long. Certification filing leaks show that the company’s already prepping a smaller “P3C” with seven tools and seven rolls of filament storage instead of nine.
Bambu Lab H3C
The H3C is a very large, very tall printer with a large build volume. Compare it to my normal size P1P.
Additionally, Bambu will let all three of its existing dual-nozzle printers print with two different sizes of nozzle by next spring, including the H2D, the H2C, and the X2D.

Yvonne Bajela is bringing $17M in fresh capital to Europe’s startup scene
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
08:01:00 UTC
17:01:00 KST

Yvonne Bajela knew it was time to launch her own fund. She spent more than a decade as a VC, most recently at LocalGlobe and Impact X Capital Partners, where she made bets on now-unicorn companies like the fintech Wise, the insurance company Marshmallow, and robotaxi Mooves.
On Tuesday, she announced that her own fund, Evertrue Capital, officially closed an oversubscribed $17 million Fund I.
“After more than a decade backing founders who bet everything on their ideas, it felt like time to make a bet of my own,” she said. “I wanted the independence to act on those convictions and build something that reflected my own approach to investing.”
The firm, which has already backed seven companies, will focus on early-stage investing across the U.K. and Europe. The average check size will be around £350,000, she said, with plans to back at least 20 companies over the next three years.
Perhaps unsurprisingly, she said this AI boom helped her realize that this was the right time to launch her own fund. Not only has it changed the economics of launching a company, she said, but it has created new opportunities for early-stage investors like herself. “The ability to build has been democratized,” she said. “But the ability to build something enduring remains rare.”
As TechCrunch has previously reported, the U.K.’s startup scene is having a moment. King’s Cross, for example, is one of the world’s top AI hubs, while companies like Revolut, Synthesia, ElevenLabs, and the Bezos-backed CuspAI are redefining what it means to scale and attract success in the U.K. market. For someone like Bajela, this moment means there is an opportunity to snap up investments in the next generation of top British talent early. “I think more globally significant businesses will emerge from a wider range of starting points,” she said.
However, this is also a tough market for emerging fund managers. In the U.S., it has been described as a barbell market where capital is concentrated at the top and among firms led by those who already have solid track records. Things may be slightly rosier in the U.K., as PitchBook data through the end of September shows that emerging fund managers in this region raised $7.4 billion, already surpassing the $6.2 billion they raised in all of 2025.
Still, Bajela said fundraising was a grind. The hardest rejections weren’t necessarily the outright nos. “They were the ones that came after months of conversations and significant time invested, only for the answer to ultimately be no,” she said. “Time is one of the most valuable resources a founder has, and a prolonged process without clarity has a real cost.”
Still, she said the fund nabbed five institutional backers, including the British Business Bank and Basecamp, the fund-of-funds of the investment firm Phoenix Court, which is also home to LocalGlobe. Evertrue was part of the £400 million British Business Bank’s Investor Pathways capital initiative, which saw it distribute £90 million to 10 first-time fund managers. Bajela said Evertrue wanted to raise around $13 million but saw a lot of investor interest. She decided to turn down additional investors rather than expand the fund size.
“Fund size is a strategic decision, not a measure of success in itself,” she said. “I wanted enough capital to build meaningful positions in my highest-conviction investments without creating pressure to deploy capital simply because it was available.”
Around 80% of Evertrue’s LPs are U.K. based, with the rest scattered across Europe, Asia, and the U.S. She said her international LP base represents the relationships she’s built “over more than a decade investing across markets.” It also reflects the fund’s global ambition, she said, especially since so many British founders keep their eyes on a U.S. expansion; more than half her portfolio already operates in the U.S.
Evertrue will invest mainly across AI and fintech, she said, adding that she’s “particularly interested in people with a unique insight into a problem, an unusual ability to execute, and the ambition to build something much bigger than their initial product.”
“I also pay attention to the distance a founder has traveled, what they’ve overcome, and how that has shaped their perspective,” she continued.
She’s lived in Japan as a senior investment manager at Mitsui and started her career as an analyst at Goldman Sachs. Throughout her career, she said she’s seen how “widely distributed ambition and talent are.”
“I want Evertrue to be known for the quality of the founders I back and the businesses they go on to build.”

Could a modern chess engine on a Pentium have defeated Kasparov in 1996?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
07:56:21 UTC
16:56:21 KST

by Nicholas Carlini 2026-11-01
On February 10th, 1996, a computer program (IBM's Deep Blue) defeated the reigning chess champion (Garry Kasparov) in a game of chess for the first time. Deep Blue would go on to lose the match, but a year later, would get its revenge in a 3.5-2.5 rematch.
In order to achieve this feat, IBM spent several million dollars on research and development building a special-purpose computer specifically for this purpose. Deep Blue itself (the victorious, upgraded version) was powered by 30 P2SC processors each running at roughly 120 MHz, and (most importantly) 480 custom VLSI chess co-processors used to perform chess-specific operations like move generation and position evaluation. When it was built, Deep Blue was the 259th most powerful supercomputer in the world, and could analyze over 200 million chess positions per second.
But was Deep Blue necessary to beat Kasparov? Or could we have gotten away with an off-the-shelf 1996 desktop running a smarter chess engine?
As it turns out, we could easily have beaten Kasparov without building Deep Blue, using only commodity hardware, and it (almost certainly) wouldn't have even been close. I know this because, as I write this very sentence, I have sitting next to me a 200 MHz Intel Pentium Pro (released exactly 31 years ago---November 1st, 1995) with 64MB of RAM running a custom port of Stockfish that plays at an estimated Elo of 3300 ± 87 at classical time controls---far beyond the strength of any human, or indeed Kasparov's Elo of just under 2800. But wait, there's more! I've hooked this machine up to the internet with a Realtek RTL8139C Ethernet card, so you can play it below!
There are three ways to get stronger at chess: you can analyze more moves, analyze better moves, or analyze moves better. Famously, humans improve by doing the latter two: the average chess grandmaster during a classical game will analyze roughly the same number of moves as an amateur player, but they analyze only the most critical moves and do a better job with that analysis. Chess engines like Stockfish, running on silicon instead of our human brains, dominate us at the first of these and analyze millions of positions per second. And because there's not that much room for micro-optimizations on modern engines that will let a given CPU process more positions per second, most progress in chess AI also tends to follow how humans improve and finds better methods for selecting moves and analyzing boards.
Skill in chess is measured by an Elo score. A difference of 200 Elo means that you should expect the stronger player to win three out of every four games, and multiplicatively from there: a 400 Elo gap corresponds to a 90% expected score and a 1000 Elo gap gives a 99.7% expected score. The best chess engines that you could run on commodity 1996 hardware were rated roughly 2300 Elo. Deep Blue was rated 2700. In contrast, modern Stockfish is rated closer to 3700.
This raises the question: how much of the advantage of a modern chess engine comes down to the fact that a modern desktop computer is extremely fast, and how much of the advantage comes down to the fact that we've just gotten better at programming chess engines? As it turns out, the majority of the Elo gains (+720 of the +1335 gained) can be attributed to better programming, and not better hardware.
To test this, I ran two experiments. The first experiment uses Crafty, a competitive engine from 1996 whose source code is now available. On my Pentium Pro, the 1996 build of Crafty version 11.13 has an Elo of 1999 ± 90 at 1 second per move, and 2383 ± 77 at 10 seconds per move. On modern hardware (a Ryzen 7) this engine's Elo jumps massively to 2614 ± 97 at the same 1 second per move. But if I take this engine and slowly start to add all the knowledge we have about how to design better chess engines---adding modern search algorithms like fail-soft, LMR, correction history; adding better quiescence methods; and adding neural-net evals (NNUE)---then you can increase the Elo up to 2718 ± 34 on the Pentium Pro at 1 second per move, and 2974 ± 74 at 10 seconds per move.
In the second experiment I go somewhat further: instead of trying to update Crafty, let's just try to get Stockfish---the best chess engine today---running on 1996 hardware and see how it does. This takes some work and is mainly a matter of rewriting the code so that it uses 32-bit arithmetic (a PPro is a 32-bit machine) and doesn't use more than 64MB of RAM. This naive port has an Elo of roughly 2496 ± 64 at 1 second per move (2940 ± 76 at 10 seconds per move). But we can do better! A modern Stockfish engine is designed to run on a modern CPU. By making a number of adjustments to the algorithm and tuning it to the Pentium, we can increase its Elo to 2846 ± 35 at 1 second per move, 3109 ± 79 at 10 seconds per move, and 3180 ± 80 at 30 seconds per move.
The most concise way to summarize all of the above is just to have them play a match of 100 games against each other. And when I do this, I find that a modern chess engine running on a 1996 Pentium Pro wins 78, draws 17, and loses 5 games against the 1996 Crafty engine running on modern hardware.
The remainder of this article provides the details.
There's not much to say about the hardware, to be honest. I bought a used ("vintage" said the listing; I feel old.) desktop PC with standard period-appropriate hardware. The desktop is running a 200 MHz Intel Pentium Pro connected to an Intel VS440FX motherboard with 64MB of SIMM RAM clocked at 66 MHz. The operating system boot off of a 1.44MB 3.5 inch floppy disk, and connect to the Internet via a Realtek RTL8139C. I also have a 1MB Trio64V+ graphics card connected over VGA to my monitor, with input coming from a PS/2 keyboard---but I don't much use either of those and instead communicate with it over a serial port connected to my modern desktop.
For those readers who may not be able to appropriately contextualize this hardware, a 200 MHz Pentium Pro sold for $1,325 at launch in November 1995, and four 16 MB SIMMs would have cost about $2,000. Add on the other peripherals, and this machine would likely have gone for about four or five thousand dollars. So it's a nice workstation, but by no means a supercomputer. However, given the rate of depreciation and the exponential rate of improvements to hardware, this same machine in 1997, when the second match occurred, would likely go for just a thousand dollars (because who would want to buy a Pentium Pro when the better-in-almost-every-way Pentium MMX was now available for just $400?)
The interface between the chess engine and the internet is a custom-built "operating system" whose sole job is to spin up the chess engine and connect it directly to the networking card. (Throughout this article, when I say "I wrote", what I really mean is "I asked an LLM to write". I used a combination of Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 to implement the code here. (This article, though, is human text.).) It's designed to be as compact as possible: the operating system (which, in fact, is more like a hypervisor, or something) is sitting on a bootable floppy disk. Its sole job is to boot the Pentium Pro into 32-bit protected mode, initialize the networking card, and await further instructions. I can then send it any arbitrary "userspace" guest program that I want into RAM and it'll boot that up and start running it. The chess program I wrote starts up a custom-built HTTP server which waits for incoming HTTP requests with a given position (as a FEN string) and maximum run time, and on each request runs the engine until the timer expires, and returns a response.
As mentioned earlier I (again: a language model) actually modified two engines. The stronger of the two is powered by Stockfish adapted to run efficiently on a thirty-year-old processor. It plays at an estimated Elo of 3300 at classical time controls Because I can't run nearly enough games at classical time controls on my single machine to get this number, I've extrapolated it from shorter time controls. I measured 3180 ± 80 at 30 seconds per move, and it gained +70 Elo per tripling of the time between 1 second to 10 seconds and 10 seconds to 30 seconds. Because a classical game gives about six minutes per move (including thinking on the opponent's turn) we should expect an Elo of 3350. Allowing for some diminishing returns, a safe estimate is an Elo of 3300. , high enough above Kasparov's 2800 Elo that we should expect Stockfish-1996 to come out ahead with a score of roughly 9/10. The (only slightly) weaker engine starts with the source code to Crafty 11.13, and is brought forward in time by adding all the lessons we've learned about how to write a better chess engine over the past thirty years.
The first engine I (read: my LLM) worked on was Crafty 11.13, its 1996 release. On this engine the LLM had to do the most work to backport ideas we've learned over the last 30 years. Below is a breakdown of where the Elo gains come from, when evaluating either at 1 second per move or 10 seconds per move. Sometimes you'll find the 1s vs 10s improvements disagree. Part of this clearly could be noise---I only ran a few hundred games which leaves a relatively large margin of error---but there is also quite a lot of signal here. Because the 1996 computer is so much slower, at 1s/move it has a very low search depth and so how fast the evaluation runs matters more than how good it is. But at larger search depths, once you stop making tactical blunders, the position evaluation becomes much more important.
On the second engine, as mentioned above, I did the inverse. I (again, read: my LLM) ported Stockfish to run on 1996 hardware, and then tweaked the parameters so that it would be better suited to lower search depth. The gains here are thus somewhat more modest, because there are no large algorithm wins that remain.
I think it's overwhelmingly likely to be the case, but it's actually a little bit more tricky of a situation than you might hope. You see, I've done a bit of sleight of hand throughout this article. The problem is that Elo scores are relative, and I've been comparing my engine's Elo to that of various Stockfish engines that have known strengths on the Computer Chess Rating Lists (CCRL). But because humans don't play against engines very frequently, there can be some small divergences between scores on the FIDE Elo ladder and the CCRL ladder, in the same way a player's FIDE Elo doesn't directly translate to their Elo on online chess. Fortunately, because I've gotten these engines to play at an Elo rating of 3200-3300, and Kasparov was rated just under 2800, there should be more than sufficient buffer to absorb any discrepancy.
But if you happen to know a 2700+ Super GM who wants to try and defeat a 2026 chess engine playing on 1996 hardware, I'd be happy to accept the challenge!
The first time we humans do anything, we rarely do it efficiently. Once we see a path that would clearly work if only we scaled it up, we do just that. Only later, after we've had the time to better understand the problem at hand, do we come to recognize that we could have achieved the same feat much more efficiently by being clever.
I mostly did this for fun, because whether I could have beaten Kasparov with commodity hardware sounded like a fun question to answer, but I also hoped it would provide a tiny bit of insight into the rate of algorithmic progress in "AI". Chess engines in 1997 were already quite advanced; after all, Alan Turing helped write the first chess program nearly fifty years earlier. So I suppose at the time it seemed plausible that maybe there weren't that many more ideas left to find. And with hindsight it's easy to see that's wrong.
Which leads to the question: just how much are we leaving on the table with modern-day "AI"---that is to say, language models. Will the advances we accrue over the next few years from software outpace the advances in hardware scale? Clearly this toy experiment doesn't answer that question definitively, but it does gesture at a potential future. (There's also probably some kind of meta-lesson about using LLMs---"AI"---to speed up our ability to answer weird research questions like this.)
(Also, uh, if anyone has any ideas for projects I could do with a Pentium Pro in a few weeks once I no longer need it to host this chess engine ... do let me know!)

====================================================================================================

In the second experiment I go somewhat further: instead of trying to update Crafty, let's just try to get Stockfish---the best chess engine today---running on 1996 hardware and see how it does. This takes some work and is mainly a matter of rewriting the code so that it uses 32-bit arithmetic (a PPro is a 32-bit machine) and doesn't use more than 64MB of RAM. This naive port has an Elo of roughly 2496 ± 64 at 1 second per move (2940 ± 76 at 10 seconds per move). But we can do better! A modern Stockfish engine is designed to run on a modern CPU. By making a number of adjustments to the algorithm and tuning it to the Pentium, we can increase its Elo to 2846 ± 35 at 1 second per move, 3109 ± 79 at 10 seconds per move, and 3180 ± 80 at 30 seconds per move.
The most concise way to summarize all of the above is just to have them play a match of 100 games against each other. And when I do this, I find that a modern chess engine running on a 1996 Pentium Pro wins 78, draws 17, and loses 5 games against the 1996 Crafty engine running on modern hardware.
The remainder of this article provides the details.
There's not much to say about the hardware, to be honest. I bought a used ("vintage" said the listing; I feel old.) desktop PC with standard period-appropriate hardware. The desktop is running a 200 MHz Intel Pentium Pro connected to an Intel VS440FX motherboard with 64MB of SIMM RAM clocked at 66 MHz. The operating system boot off of a 1.44MB 3.5 inch floppy disk, and connect to the Internet via a Realtek RTL8139C. I also have a 1MB Trio64V+ graphics card connected over VGA to my monitor, with input coming from a PS/2 keyboard---but I don't much use either of those and instead communicate with it over a serial port connected to my modern desktop.
For those readers who may not be able to appropriately contextualize this hardware, a 200 MHz Pentium Pro sold for $1,325 at launch in November 1995, and four 16 MB SIMMs would have cost about $2,000. Add on the other peripherals, and this machine would likely have gone for about four or five thousand dollars. So it's a nice workstation, but by no means a supercomputer. However, given the rate of depreciation and the exponential rate of improvements to hardware, this same machine in 1997, when the second match occurred, would likely go for just a thousand dollars (because who would want to buy a Pentium Pro when the better-in-almost-every-way Pentium MMX was now available for just $400?)
The interface between the chess engine and the internet is a custom-built "operating system" whose sole job is to spin up the chess engine and connect it directly to the networking card. (Throughout this article, when I say "I wrote", what I really mean is "I asked an LLM to write". I used a combination of Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, and GPT-6 to implement the code here. (This article, though, is human text.).) It's designed to be as compact as possible: the operating system (which, in fact, is more like a hypervisor, or something) is sitting on a bootable floppy disk. Its sole job is to boot the Pentium Pro into 32-bit protected mode, initialize the networking card, and await further instructions. I can then send it any arbitrary "userspace" guest program that I want into RAM and it'll boot that up and start running it. The chess program I wrote starts up a custom-built HTTP server which waits for incoming HTTP requests with a given position (as a FEN string) and maximum run time, and on each request runs the engine until the timer expires, and returns a response.
As mentioned earlier I (again: a language model) actually modified two engines. The stronger of the two is powered by Stockfish adapted to run efficiently on a thirty-year-old processor. It plays at an estimated Elo of 3300 at classical time controls Because I can't run nearly enough games at classical time controls on my single machine to get this number, I've extrapolated it from shorter time controls. I measured 3180 ± 80 at 30 seconds per move, and it gained +70 Elo per tripling of the time between 1 second to 10 seconds and 10 seconds to 30 seconds. Because a classical game gives about six minutes per move (including thinking on the opponent's turn) we should expect an Elo of 3350. Allowing for some diminishing returns, a safe estimate is an Elo of 3300. , high enough above Kasparov's 2800 Elo that we should expect Stockfish-1996 to come out ahead with a score of roughly 9/10. The (only slightly) weaker engine starts with the source code to Crafty 11.13, and is brought forward in time by adding all the lessons we've learned about how to write a better chess engine over the past thirty years.
The first engine I (read: my LLM) worked on was Crafty 11.13, its 1996 release. On this engine the LLM had to do the most work to backport ideas we've learned over the last 30 years. Below is a breakdown of where the Elo gains come from, when evaluating either at 1 second per move or 10 seconds per move. Sometimes you'll find the 1s vs 10s improvements disagree. Part of this clearly could be noise---I only ran a few hundred games which leaves a relatively large margin of error---but there is also quite a lot of signal here. Because the 1996 computer is so much slower, at 1s/move it has a very low search depth and so how fast the evaluation runs matters more than how good it is. But at larger search depths, once you stop making tactical blunders, the position evaluation becomes much more important.
On the second engine, as mentioned above, I did the inverse. I (again, read: my LLM) ported Stockfish to run on 1996 hardware, and then tweaked the parameters so that it would be better suited to lower search depth. The gains here are thus somewhat more modest, because there are no large algorithm wins that remain.
I think it's overwhelmingly likely to be the case, but it's actually a little bit more tricky of a situation than you might hope. You see, I've done a bit of sleight of hand throughout this article. The problem is that Elo scores are relative, and I've been comparing my engine's Elo to that of various Stockfish engines that have known strengths on the Computer Chess Rating Lists (CCRL). But because humans don't play against engines very frequently, there can be some small divergences between scores on the FIDE Elo ladder and the CCRL ladder, in the same way a player's FIDE Elo doesn't directly translate to their Elo on online chess. Fortunately, because I've gotten these engines to play at an Elo rating of 3200-3300, and Kasparov was rated just under 2800, there should be more than sufficient buffer to absorb any discrepancy.
But if you happen to know a 2700+ Super GM who wants to try and defeat a 2026 chess engine playing on 1996 hardware, I'd be happy to accept the challenge!
The first time we humans do anything, we rarely do it efficiently. Once we see a path that would clearly work if only we scaled it up, we do just that. Only later, after we've had the time to better understand the problem at hand, do we come to recognize that we could have achieved the same feat much more efficiently by being clever.
I mostly did this for fun, because whether I could have beaten Kasparov with commodity hardware sounded like a fun question to answer, but I also hoped it would provide a tiny bit of insight into the rate of algorithmic progress in "AI". Chess engines in 1997 were already quite advanced; after all, Alan Turing helped write the first chess program nearly fifty years earlier. So I suppose at the time it seemed plausible that maybe there weren't that many more ideas left to find. And with hindsight it's easy to see that's wrong.
Which leads to the question: just how much are we leaving on the table with modern-day "AI"---that is to say, language models. Will the advances we accrue over the next few years from software outpace the advances in hardware scale? Clearly this toy experiment doesn't answer that question definitively, but it does gesture at a potential future. (There's also probably some kind of meta-lesson about using LLMs---"AI"---to speed up our ability to answer weird research questions like this.)
(Also, uh, if anyone has any ideas for projects I could do with a Pentium Pro in a few weeks once I no longer need it to host this chess engine ... do let me know!)

uBlock Origin filter to block autoplay videos in TechCrunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
07:36:47 UTC
16:36:47 KST

Every TechCrunch article autoplays a video in the middle of the post. Hiding it isn’t enough, because the player keeps running in the background.
The video is a JW Player embed, and the page also loads Connatix’s floating ad player. Blocking their scripts stops the video from loading at all, and the cosmetic rules hide the empty box it leaves behind.
These work in uBlock Origin on Firefox (the full MV2 version, not uBO Lite). Paste them into Dashboard → My filters and click Apply changes:
! TechCrunch: stop the autoplaying JW Player video
||content.jwplatform.com/libraries/$script,domain=techcrunch.com
||ssl.p.jwpcdn.com^$script,domain=techcrunch.com
||connatix.com^$third-party,domain=techcrunch.com
techcrunch.com##.wp-block-techcrunch-jw-player-embed
techcrunch.com##.jw-player-inline-promo
If TechCrunch switches video vendors, the ## rules will probably keep hiding
the box, but you’ll need a new network rule to stop the audio.

Apple Watch’s AI features for rewinding and recapping conversations begin beta testing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
07:20:00 UTC
16:20:00 KST

Apple’s AI-powered “Audio Intelligence” technology for the Apple Watch is rolling out into beta testing on Tuesday, initially for developers in the iOS 27.3 update, after first being announced at the company’s Surprise and Shine hardware event in September. The technology includes a set of four opt-in AI features that allow Apple Watch Series 12 wearers to detect important sounds, identify songs, catch up on conversations, and take notes.
The news was first announced via an emailed press release sent out by Apple’s communications team in India early on Tuesday. The update rolled out in the U.S. and other markets later in the day.
The sound recognition feature will help deaf and hard-of-hearing users identify important sounds like sirens, alarms, or doorbells from their watch, while the song recognition feature taps into Apple’s Shazam app to detect music playing in the background and identify the song name and artist.
However, the more potentially controversial features are those that listen to human conversations: Live Rewind and Siri Recaps.
Given the backlash to AI recording devices, like Meta’s AI glasses and other AI wearables, Apple has attempted to carve out a space where the features can be useful to Apple Watch owners, while still respecting the privacy of those around them.
With Live Rewind, the idea is to let you go back in time to see what someone just said, in case you missed it. For instance, if someone was giving you verbal directions or reading a long list of specials at a restaurant, you could double-press on the Watch’s digital crown to see what was said in the last 15 seconds as a text snippet displayed on the watch face. You can view this snippet and then do nothing, and it will disappear permanently. Or you can save it to the stand-alone Siri app that shipped with iOS 27 for later access, which might be helpful if you’re trying to remember someone’s name or take a quick note from a fast-paced presentation.
Apple says that users will also be able to tap an “Ask Siri” option that appears below the text snippet if they have questions about something that was said — like a technical term they don’t understand, or perhaps some sauce option the waiter mentioned that they’re unfamiliar with, among other things.
When you double-press the digital crown, an audible chime appears and an animation displays on the watch. This is meant to signal to people through the combination of the gesture, sound, and visual display that you’ve recorded something that was said.
These snippets will be deleted automatically after 30 seconds if you don’t save them.
The other option, Siri Recaps, takes this ambient listening technology even further by allowing Apple Watch owners to take high-level notes of their conversations.
Importantly, Apple says it’s not identifying speakers, saving the raw audio, or providing word-for-word transcriptions. Instead, the feature summarizes a conversation with a short sentence and some bullet points that identify key points. For instance, depending on the topic, the bullet points might include things like important dates or deadlines, pricing or payment plan information, and other factual information.
Apple suggested the feature could be used in scenarios like work meetings, parent-teacher conferences, personal training sessions, or other places where you may need to remember what tasks you have to complete or things that were said. Essentially, it’s supposed to mimic a user’s ability to jot down their own notes — without adding emotion or tone.
This could be helpful particularly at times when you aren’t able to write up your own notes, either because your hands are full or you’re trying to concentrate on whatever’s being said at the time. The recaps won’t record conversations when you’re listening to music with your headphones or using their noise cancellation features.
At the end of the day, you’re prompted to review your saved Siri Recaps when the feature is enabled, and then choose which, if any, you want to save. These notes can be saved to your Notes app or even exported to your Journal app, if they’re more personal in nature. If you do nothing, the recaps will delete themselves within seven days.
This reminder to review the Siri Recaps you’ve recorded also appears when you first unlock your Apple Watch in the morning.
Users can opt to enable the Siri Recaps manually, or they can configure a schedule, such as only having the recapping take place while at work, or making sure that they never run at night. Even if they’re running on a schedule, you can still turn off the recapping feature at any time from the Control Center.
Apple notes that Siri Recaps has been designed to omit sensitive information like government-assigned identifiers, financial and authentication data, certain personal identifiers, and any language that would promote self-harm.
The Audio Intelligence features for the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 rely on a combination of Apple’s hardware, software, and services. This includes the S11 chip, built-in microphone, and the Apple Intelligence models that run on the iPhone, as well as Apple’s Private Cloud Compute.
The always-on processor includes a secure enclave — a hardware-protected memory space that can’t be accessed by the rest of the operating system — where a dedicated audio buffer processes the raw audio. This allows the audio to be processed without it actually being accessible to anyone, including Apple. The audio is only accessible to the paired iPhone through a secure pairing mechanism between it and the watch.
To work, lightweight AI models on the S11 chip on the Apple Watch detect if there’s a conversation happening that the wearer is a part of, which is then transferred to the secure enclave on the iPhone. On-device processing on the iPhone turns the audio into condensed text, meaning the text of the conversation with the filler words removed. This condensed text is then encrypted and sent to Apple’s Private Cloud Compute (PCC) to create the recap of the conversation that is sent back to the phone. (The recap and any summarizations used to create it are deleted from PCC immediately afterwards.)
The recaps you can then access on your iPhone are only accessible to you, not to Apple. And they’re encrypted when they’re synced between your multiple Apple devices.
Similarly, Apple Watch transfers audio to the iPhone for processing to create the 15-second snippets for Live Rewind.
Apple says none of these features should impact the battery life of your watch or phone. The features will later roll out to the public beta for broader testing before becoming publicly available to all.
Post updated after publication to indicate the current status of the software’s rollout.

Nvidia – open-source auto-ontology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
07:04:50 UTC
16:04:50 KST

An open context layer that helps agents give fewer wrong answers on enterprise data.
Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability is what gates agentic analytics: a revenue figure delivered faster is worth nothing if it's wrong. Before an agent queries, it needs to know where the data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar.
Auto-Ontology is a service you run next to your databases to give agents that context. It compiles their metadata into an ontology: business terms mapped to columns, reviewed SQL for measures, and the relationships between tables. Agents query through the ontology, and people review it in a web UI. It complements the semantic models you already own.
With Auto-Ontology, developers can:
- Discover. Generate an ontology from database metadata, import existing semantic models, and explore the result as a semantic graph.
- Ground. Give agents one definition per business concept, mapped across tables and databases.
- Certify. Review, edit, and certify definitions in the UI or through the API.
- Validate. Check whether a question is answerable before querying, and return the SQL and the agent's steps with each answer.
- Expose. Serve context to any agent harness through MCP, agent skills, and a REST API.
The usual shortcut is to paste the schema into the agent's context window. Auto-Ontology gives the agent tools over the ontology:
The companion repository, auto-ontology-eval, measures ontology performance on benchmarks and evals.
For BIRD, BEAVER, FDABench-Lite, and Wide World Importers, each eval item pairs a question with gold SQL, and a run asks every question of the same model twice:
- Control. The model gets the database schema in its prompt.
- Treatment. Auto-Ontology's question-answering agent, the one behind Chat, works from the compiled ontology.
A deterministic verifier scores the SQL from each arm by execution match, using each benchmark's official rule where it has one. The report gives the accuracy difference and lists the questions the ontology fixed and the ones it broke. BIRD-Interact, a multi-turn benchmark where the agent asks clarifying questions, runs on its own harness.
To run the comparison on BIRD, follow the auto-ontology-eval setup, then run:
uv run python main.py --database-name bird
This runs Auto-Ontology with Docker Compose against Wide World Importers,
Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2,
uv, and an NVIDIA API key (nvapi-...) from
build.nvidia.com.
- Clone the repository and create .env:
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology cp .env.example .env Then set these values in .env:

AUTH_SECRET=<a long random string, e.g. from openssl rand -base64 32> APP_URL=http://localhost:3000 POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<a new password> CONNECTION_STRINGS=postgresql://postgres:<the same password>@postgres:5432/wideworldimporters AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password> PGADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password> Compose publishes Postgres, pgAdmin, and the web app on the host, so replace
each default password before you start it. .env.example also sets an API
key per model role: replace each nvapi-your-api-key-here with your key, or
delete those lines so they fall back to DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY.
- Start Postgres and load the sample database. The seed script lives in auto-ontology-eval; pass it the Postgres password you set: docker compose up -d --wait postgres git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology-eval.git ../auto-ontology-eval (cd ../auto-ontology-eval && uv sync && cp .env.example .env && \ POSTGRES_PASSWORD='<the same password>' \ uv run python scripts/seed/seed_wwi.py --database-name wideworldimporters --drop)

- Open http://localhost:3000 and sign in with AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_EMAIL and AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD from .env. Go to Settings → Semantic
Compilation and turn it on. Ingestion runs at startup; compilation starts
immediately and reports Semantic compilation is ready when it finishes.
- Ask a question in Chat: What was revenue for the USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in June 2015? The agent resolves revenue, product, and state to terms in the ontology, follows their relationships to the joins it needs, and runs the query. The answer comes back with its SQL and the steps that produced it, so you can check the result against the source: Answer:  Revenue for USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in
         June 2015 was $588.80, from 3 invoice lines.
SQL:     SELECT SUM(il.extendedprice) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS invoice_lines
         FROM sales.invoicelines il
         JOIN sales.invoices i             ON il.invoiceid = i.invoiceid
         JOIN warehouse.stockitems si      ON il.stockitemid = si.stockitemid
         JOIN sales.customers c            ON i.customerid = c.customerid
         JOIN application.cities ct        ON c.deliverycityid = ct.cityid
         JOIN application.stateprovinces sp ON ct.stateprovinceid = sp.stateprovinceid
         WHERE si.stockitemname = 'USB food flash drive - sushi roll'
           AND sp.stateprovincename = 'Pennsylvania'
           AND i.invoicedate >= '2015-06-01' AND i.invoicedate < '2015-07-01'
Steps:   Resolved terms: Invoice Line (revenue), Stock Item, State Province, Invoice
         Joined: invoice line -> invoice -> customer -> city -> state province
         Validated the filter values against the data, then executed
- Ask something the data can't answer. Wide World Importers has no advertising data, so a question about ad spend has nothing to resolve against. An agent connected through MCP checks answerability first and asks you to clarify: You:    What was return on ad spend for the sushi roll flash drive in June 2015?
Agent:  check_answerable -> coverage 0.5; no term covers "ad spend"
Agent:  I can find revenue for that product, but this data has no
        advertising spend, so I can't compute return on ad spend. Do you
        want June 2015 revenue instead, or is ad spend tracked in another
        source I should connect?
If the UI loads without its left navigation after a restart, the browser is
holding a stale session cookie. Clear site data for localhost:3000 and sign in
again. For other setup failures, see the
setup skill's troubleshooting guide.
Auto-Ontology works in three stages: it generates an ontology, people certify it, and the agent answers questions from it.
The ontology holds three kinds of definition:
- Terms. Business concepts such as Customer or Invoice Line, each with a description and synonyms, mapped to the columns that hold them.
- SQL attributes. Reviewed SQL expressions under a term, such as a margin or a rolling total. The agent reuses them, so answers compute each measure the same way.
- Relationships. How tables join, including bridge tables, inferred from keys and from the data.
Generate. The ingestion service builds a first draft from the source databases:
- Read sources: extract schemas, profile columns, and sample values into the catalog.
- Name entities: extract terms table by table and map each to columns.
- Resolve relationships: infer joins between tables and bridge tables, and suggest SQL attributes from query history.
- Write the ontology: store terms, relationships, and SQL attributes in Postgres, with embeddings in pgvector for retrieval.
The result is a semantic graph you can explore in the UI. In this example, one compilation of Wide World Importers produced 31 terms; selecting Order shows its description, related terms, mapped columns, and SQL attributes:
Certify. People make the draft trustworthy:
- Test with real questions in Chat, or with check_answerable and ask_question over MCP.
- Refine terms, descriptions, and SQL attributes in the UI or through the API.
- Certify names, descriptions, and SQL attributes once they're correct.
Answer. For each question, the agent:
- Classifies the intent and extracts the entities the question names.
- Retrieves candidate terms, columns, and SQL attributes by embedding search.
- Writes SQL from those candidates.
- Checks the filter values and the query against the database, repairing the SQL when a check fails.
- Runs the query and returns the answer with its SQL and the steps it took.
When the candidates can't support a query, the agent reports that the question can't be answered from this data. Predictive questions go to KumoRFM when it's configured (see Predictions).
In Chat, each answer shows its SQL, and you can view the rows, download them as CSV, or read them as a chart:
Auto-Ontology is compatible with Apache Ossie, the
open standard for exchanging semantic models. Ossie includes a
converter for Auto-Ontology,
which Auto-Ontology uses to import and export model definitions as Ossie YAML.
Use Settings → Import / Export, or POST /api/model/import and
POST /api/model/export.
Keep ports 3001 and 3002 on a private network. FastAPI trusts the user identity
the frontend forwards in the x-auto-ontology-user-id header, and the ingestion
service's endpoints (ingest, delete, reset, compile) have no authentication of
their own. Clients go through the web app on port 3000.
The MCP server gives any MCP client read-only tools over the ontology. Each user signs in through Auto-Ontology, and every call runs with that user's permissions.
Run the server against your deployment:
AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_URL=http://localhost:3000 \
  uvx --from "git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git#subdirectory=mcp" auto-ontology-mcp
Cursor (~/.cursor/mcp.json):
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "auto-ontology": { "url": "http://localhost:3003/mcp" }
  }
}
Claude Desktop (claude_desktop_config.json), bridged with
mcp-remote:
{
  "mcpServers": {

      "command": "npx",

Restart the client after editing its config, then sign in when it prompts. Sign-in, configuration, and troubleshooting are in docs/mcp.md.
Three skills teach a coding agent to work with Auto-Ontology. Start at AGENTS.md.
Ask a question with POST /api/chat/completions on the web app's origin. Mint
an API token under the user menu → API Tokens. The response is a
server-sent event stream: a result event carries the answer, and
data: [DONE] ends the stream.
curl -N http://localhost:3000/api/chat/completions \
  -H "x-api-key: $AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"}'import json
import os
import requests
response = requests.post(
    "http://localhost:3000/api/chat/completions",
    headers={"x-api-key": os.environ["AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN"]},
    json={"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"},
    stream=True,
    timeout=900,
)
response.raise_for_status()
for line in response.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True):
    if not line or not line.startswith("data:"):
        continue
    payload = line.removeprefix("data:").strip()
    if payload == "[DONE]":
        break
    event = json.loads(payload)
    if event["type"] == "result":
        print(event["answer"]["response"])
        print(event["answer"]["sql_code"])
    elif event["type"] == "error":
        raise RuntimeError(event["message"])
Event types, multi-turn conversations, and the gateway trust boundary are in docs/conversation-api.md. Every other operation is in the OpenAPI spec.
Auto-Ontology connects to ten engines:
- PostgreSQL
- MySQL
- Databricks
- Snowflake
- ClickHouse
- Trino
- Apache Kyuubi
- HeavyDB
- DuckDB
- SQLite
Add connections under Settings → Connections, or list them in
CONNECTION_STRINGS. DuckDB and SQLite are connection-string only. See

credential storage.
Auto-Ontology uses four model roles. With an nvapi- key, each defaults to an
NVIDIA NIM on build.nvidia.com:
To use self-hosted NIM or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, set
<ROLE>_ENDPOINT, <ROLE>_API_KEY, and <ROLE>_MODEL. Any field you leave
unset falls back to DEFAULT_MODELS_<FIELD>, so the simplest setup fills in
DEFAULT_MODELS_* and overrides only what differs. Use models
that support structured output, and keep the embedding model the same for
ingestion and queries. .env.example documents every
variable.
Set KUMO_RFM_API_KEY and the agent routes predictive questions to KumoRFM.
KumoRFM is a hosted service: to answer, the agent uploads the connected tables
to it, capped by KUMO_MAX_TABLES (20 by default) and
KUMO_MAX_ROWS_PER_TABLE (unlimited unless set). Review what that sends, and
complete your organization's data review, before you enable it.

Nvidia – open-source auto-ontology
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
07:04:50 UTC
16:04:50 KST

An open context layer that helps agents give fewer wrong answers on enterprise data.
Agents can retrieve documents and query databases, but reliability is what gates agentic analytics: a revenue figure delivered faster is worth nothing if it's wrong. Before an agent queries, it needs to know where the data lives, what it means, whether to use it, how to use it, where it came from, and what is similar.
Auto-Ontology is a service you run next to your databases to give agents that context. It compiles their metadata into an ontology: business terms mapped to columns, reviewed SQL for measures, and the relationships between tables. Agents query through the ontology, and people review it in a web UI. It complements the semantic models you already own.
With Auto-Ontology, developers can:
- Discover. Generate an ontology from database metadata, import existing semantic models, and explore the result as a semantic graph.
- Ground. Give agents one definition per business concept, mapped across tables and databases.
- Certify. Review, edit, and certify definitions in the UI or through the API.
- Validate. Check whether a question is answerable before querying, and return the SQL and the agent's steps with each answer.
- Expose. Serve context to any agent harness through MCP, agent skills, and a REST API.
The usual shortcut is to paste the schema into the agent's context window. Auto-Ontology gives the agent tools over the ontology:
The companion repository, auto-ontology-eval, measures ontology performance on benchmarks and evals.
For BIRD, BEAVER, FDABench-Lite, and Wide World Importers, each eval item pairs a question with gold SQL, and a run asks every question of the same model twice:
- Control. The model gets the database schema in its prompt.
- Treatment. Auto-Ontology's question-answering agent, the one behind Chat, works from the compiled ontology.
A deterministic verifier scores the SQL from each arm by execution match, using each benchmark's official rule where it has one. The report gives the accuracy difference and lists the questions the ontology fixed and the ones it broke. BIRD-Interact, a multi-turn benchmark where the agent asks clarifying questions, runs on its own harness.
To run the comparison on BIRD, follow the auto-ontology-eval setup, then run:
uv run python main.py --database-name bird
This runs Auto-Ontology with Docker Compose against Wide World Importers,
Microsoft's sample sales database. You need Docker with Compose v2,
uv, and an NVIDIA API key (nvapi-...) from
build.nvidia.com.
- Clone the repository and create .env:
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git && cd auto-ontology cp .env.example .env Then set these values in .env:
DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY=nvapi-... AUTH_SECRET=<a long random string, e.g. from openssl rand -base64 32> APP_URL=http://localhost:3000 POSTGRES_PASSWORD=<a new password> CONNECTION_STRINGS=postgresql://postgres:<the same password>@postgres:5432/wideworldimporters AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password> PGADMIN_PASSWORD=<a new password> Compose publishes Postgres, pgAdmin, and the web app on the host, so replace
each default password before you start it. .env.example also sets an API
key per model role: replace each nvapi-your-api-key-here with your key, or
delete those lines so they fall back to DEFAULT_MODELS_API_KEY.
- Start Postgres and load the sample database. The seed script lives in auto-ontology-eval; pass it the Postgres password you set: docker compose up -d --wait postgres git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology-eval.git ../auto-ontology-eval (cd ../auto-ontology-eval && uv sync && cp .env.example .env && \ POSTGRES_PASSWORD='<the same password>' \ uv run python scripts/seed/seed_wwi.py --database-name wideworldimporters --drop)
- Build and start the rest of the stack: docker compose up -d --build
- Open http://localhost:3000 and sign in with AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_EMAIL and AUTO_ONTOLOGY_ADMIN_PASSWORD from .env. Go to Settings → Semantic
Compilation and turn it on. Ingestion runs at startup; compilation starts
immediately and reports Semantic compilation is ready when it finishes.
- Ask a question in Chat: What was revenue for the USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in June 2015? The agent resolves revenue, product, and state to terms in the ontology, follows their relationships to the joins it needs, and runs the query. The answer comes back with its SQL and the steps that produced it, so you can check the result against the source: Answer:  Revenue for USB food flash drive - sushi roll in Pennsylvania in
         June 2015 was $588.80, from 3 invoice lines.
SQL:     SELECT SUM(il.extendedprice) AS revenue, COUNT(*) AS invoice_lines
         FROM sales.invoicelines il
         JOIN sales.invoices i             ON il.invoiceid = i.invoiceid
         JOIN warehouse.stockitems si      ON il.stockitemid = si.stockitemid
         JOIN sales.customers c            ON i.customerid = c.customerid
         JOIN application.cities ct        ON c.deliverycityid = ct.cityid
         JOIN application.stateprovinces sp ON ct.stateprovinceid = sp.stateprovinceid
         WHERE si.stockitemname = 'USB food flash drive - sushi roll'
           AND sp.stateprovincename = 'Pennsylvania'
           AND i.invoicedate >= '2015-06-01' AND i.invoicedate < '2015-07-01'
Steps:   Resolved terms: Invoice Line (revenue), Stock Item, State Province, Invoice
         Joined: invoice line -> invoice -> customer -> city -> state province
         Validated the filter values against the data, then executed
- Ask something the data can't answer. Wide World Importers has no advertising data, so a question about ad spend has nothing to resolve against. An agent connected through MCP checks answerability first and asks you to clarify: You:    What was return on ad spend for the sushi roll flash drive in June 2015?
Agent:  check_answerable -> coverage 0.5; no term covers "ad spend"
Agent:  I can find revenue for that product, but this data has no
        advertising spend, so I can't compute return on ad spend. Do you
        want June 2015 revenue instead, or is ad spend tracked in another
        source I should connect?
If the UI loads without its left navigation after a restart, the browser is
holding a stale session cookie. Clear site data for localhost:3000 and sign in
again. For other setup failures, see the
setup skill's troubleshooting guide.
Auto-Ontology works in three stages: it generates an ontology, people certify it, and the agent answers questions from it.
The ontology holds three kinds of definition:
- Terms. Business concepts such as Customer or Invoice Line, each with a description and synonyms, mapped to the columns that hold them.
- SQL attributes. Reviewed SQL expressions under a term, such as a margin or a rolling total. The agent reuses them, so answers compute each measure the same way.
- Relationships. How tables join, including bridge tables, inferred from keys and from the data.
Generate. The ingestion service builds a first draft from the source databases:
- Read sources: extract schemas, profile columns, and sample values into the catalog.
- Name entities: extract terms table by table and map each to columns.
- Resolve relationships: infer joins between tables and bridge tables, and suggest SQL attributes from query history.
- Write the ontology: store terms, relationships, and SQL attributes in Postgres, with embeddings in pgvector for retrieval.
The result is a semantic graph you can explore in the UI. In this example, one compilation of Wide World Importers produced 31 terms; selecting Order shows its description, related terms, mapped columns, and SQL attributes:
Certify. People make the draft trustworthy:
- Test with real questions in Chat, or with check_answerable and ask_question over MCP.
- Refine terms, descriptions, and SQL attributes in the UI or through the API.
- Certify names, descriptions, and SQL attributes once they're correct.
Answer. For each question, the agent:
- Classifies the intent and extracts the entities the question names.
- Retrieves candidate terms, columns, and SQL attributes by embedding search.
- Writes SQL from those candidates.
- Checks the filter values and the query against the database, repairing the SQL when a check fails.
- Runs the query and returns the answer with its SQL and the steps it took.
When the candidates can't support a query, the agent reports that the question can't be answered from this data. Predictive questions go to KumoRFM when it's configured (see Predictions).
In Chat, each answer shows its SQL, and you can view the rows, download them as CSV, or read them as a chart:
Auto-Ontology is compatible with Apache Ossie, the
open standard for exchanging semantic models. Ossie includes a
converter for Auto-Ontology,
which Auto-Ontology uses to import and export model definitions as Ossie YAML.
Use Settings → Import / Export, or POST /api/model/import and
POST /api/model/export.
Keep ports 3001 and 3002 on a private network. FastAPI trusts the user identity
the frontend forwards in the x-auto-ontology-user-id header, and the ingestion
service's endpoints (ingest, delete, reset, compile) have no authentication of
their own. Clients go through the web app on port 3000.
The MCP server gives any MCP client read-only tools over the ontology. Each user signs in through Auto-Ontology, and every call runs with that user's permissions.
Run the server against your deployment:
AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_URL=http://localhost:3000 \
  uvx --from "git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/auto-ontology.git#subdirectory=mcp" auto-ontology-mcp
Cursor (~/.cursor/mcp.json):
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "auto-ontology": { "url": "http://localhost:3003/mcp" }
  }
}
Claude Desktop (claude_desktop_config.json), bridged with
mcp-remote:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "auto-ontology": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["mcp-remote", "http://localhost:3003/mcp"]
    }
  }
}
Restart the client after editing its config, then sign in when it prompts. Sign-in, configuration, and troubleshooting are in docs/mcp.md.
Three skills teach a coding agent to work with Auto-Ontology. Start at AGENTS.md.
Ask a question with POST /api/chat/completions on the web app's origin. Mint
an API token under the user menu → API Tokens. The response is a
server-sent event stream: a result event carries the answer, and
data: [DONE] ends the stream.
curl -N http://localhost:3000/api/chat/completions \
  -H "x-api-key: $AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"}'import json
import os
import requests
response = requests.post(
    "http://localhost:3000/api/chat/completions",
    headers={"x-api-key": os.environ["AUTO_ONTOLOGY_API_TOKEN"]},
    json={"question": "How many orders shipped last week?"},
    stream=True,
    timeout=900,
)
response.raise_for_status()
for line in response.iter_lines(decode_unicode=True):
    if not line or not line.startswith("data:"):
        continue
    payload = line.removeprefix("data:").strip()
    if payload == "[DONE]":
        break
    event = json.loads(payload)
    if event["type"] == "result":
        print(event["answer"]["response"])
        print(event["answer"]["sql_code"])
    elif event["type"] == "error":
        raise RuntimeError(event["message"])
Event types, multi-turn conversations, and the gateway trust boundary are in docs/conversation-api.md. Every other operation is in the OpenAPI spec.
Auto-Ontology connects to ten engines:
- PostgreSQL
- MySQL
- Databricks
- Snowflake
- ClickHouse
- Trino
- Apache Kyuubi
- HeavyDB
- DuckDB
- SQLite
Add connections under Settings → Connections, or list them in
CONNECTION_STRINGS. DuckDB and SQLite are connection-string only. See
docs/connections.md for URL schemes, scoping, and
credential storage.
Auto-Ontology uses four model roles. With an nvapi- key, each defaults to an
NVIDIA NIM on build.nvidia.com:
To use self-hosted NIM or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, set
<ROLE>_ENDPOINT, <ROLE>_API_KEY, and <ROLE>_MODEL. Any field you leave
unset falls back to DEFAULT_MODELS_<FIELD>, so the simplest setup fills in
DEFAULT_MODELS_* and overrides only what differs. Use models
that support structured output, and keep the embedding model the same for
ingestion and queries. .env.example documents every
variable.
Set KUMO_RFM_API_KEY and the agent routes predictive questions to KumoRFM.
KumoRFM is a hosted service: to answer, the agent uploads the connected tables
to it, capped by KUMO_MAX_TABLES (20 by default) and
KUMO_MAX_ROWS_PER_TABLE (unlimited unless set). Review what that sends, and
complete your organization's data review, before you enable it.
To integrate an agent platform, application, or storage provider with Auto-Ontology, open an integration request.
The Auto-Ontology team maintains the code and doesn't accept external pull requests. Integration requests and bug reports are welcome as issues. Report security vulnerabilities through SECURITY.md. Maintainer workflow is in CONTRIBUTING.md.

China Publicly Discloses Plan For a Lunar Landing Within Three Years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-11-03
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

China Publicly Discloses Plan For a Lunar Landing Within Three Years (arstechnica.com) 60
			
		 	
				At the Seventh Manned Spaceflight Conference in Beijing, Chinese space officials publicly outlined the most detailed roadmap yet for landing astronauts on the Moon "before 2030." Ars Technica reports:  China's lunar landings will involve a lunar-orbit rendezvous similar to what NASA did in the 1960s and early 1970s with the Apollo program. However, lacking a rocket as powerful as the Saturn V vehicle, the crew and lunar lander will launch separately to the Moon. According to slides shared on social media, the current plan involves:
- An uncrewed test of the Long March 10A rocket (a single-stick variant, with no boosters) and the Mengzhou spacecraft to low-Earth orbit. Target: early 2027
- An uncrewed test of the larger Long March 10 rocket (a core stage with two boosters) and the Lanyue lunar lander, including descent/ascent from Moon's surface. Target: 2028
- A concurrent launch of two Long March 10 rockets, one carrying uncrewed Mengzhou and the other the Lanyue vehicle; they will dock in lunar orbit. Target: 2029
- Dual launch of Long March 10 rockets, this time with crew on the Mengzhou spacecraft, leading to crewed landing mission. Target: "Before 2030"
The public release of this new information provides a timeline for gauging China's technical progress in its efforts to land humans on the Moon before 2030 and beat NASA and the United States back to the lunar surface. Notably, the plan (for now, at least) omits a mission similar to Apollo 8 or Artemis II, which involved a crew flying out to the Moon and either entering orbit or passing close by before returning to Earth. The Mengzhou vehicle should still get a workout closer to Earth with humans on board as part of missions carrying astronauts to Tiangong, China's space station in low-Earth orbit.
